questions.stem: Pupils stand in lines on Monday morning. They sing one song for the whole country. Which song is it?
hints: Think about the song for all of Ghana.
It is sung at assembly.
questions.explanation: The National Anthem is the song for the whole country. It is sung at school assembly and on important national days. The other songs are for birthdays, bedtime or play.
questions.misconception: Any song can be sung at assembly.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: Ama is six years old today. Her friends want to sing a song for her. Which song fits best?
hints: Think about the name of the day.
The song has her name in it.
questions.explanation: Happy Birthday to You is sung at birthday parties. A lullaby is for babies at bedtime, a work song is for working, and the National Anthem is for the country.
questions.misconception: Any familiar song fits any occasion.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: You are singing a happy song with your class. What should you do?
hints: Happy songs make people feel good.
Use your hands and face.
questions.explanation: A happy song is sung with a happy face, clapping and maybe dancing. Crying, looking sad or sleeping are expressions for sad, quiet or sleepy songs.
questions.misconception: Any action is fine for any song.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: Kofi sings: 'Twinkle, twinkle, little star, how I wonder what you are.' Which song is Kofi singing?
hints: The first words of the song are in the question.
It is about a star in the sky.
questions.explanation: The words 'Twinkle, twinkle, little star' are the first line of the song Twinkle Twinkle Little Star. The other songs are about the country, working, or a baby.
questions.misconception: The first line does not tell you the song.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: A song says: 'Rain, rain, go away, come again another day.' What is the song about?
hints: Listen to the first word of the song.
It falls from the sky.
questions.explanation: The song talks about rain and asks it to go away. So the song is about rain, not the sun, a car or a dog.
questions.misconception: The song is about anything the child likes.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: How should pupils sing the National Anthem at assembly?
hints: It is a song for the whole country.
It shows respect.
questions.explanation: The National Anthem is sung standing still and solemnly to show respect for Ghana. Dancing, shouting or playing during the anthem is not respectful.
questions.misconception: The National Anthem is a happy party song.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: A mother sings softly to her baby at night to help the baby sleep. What kind of song is she singing?
hints: It is sung softly at bedtime.
It helps a baby sleep.
questions.explanation: A lullaby is a soft song sung to babies at bedtime to help them sleep. The National Anthem, birthday songs and work songs are for other times.
questions.misconception: All soft songs are the same.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: A song says: 'Kofi has a little dog, its name is Pat.' Who is in the song?
hints: Listen for the names in the song.
One is a boy and one is an animal.
questions.explanation: The song names Kofi and his dog Pat. Ama, the teacher and the farmer are not in this song.
questions.misconception: Any name fits the song.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: A song says: 'Share your food, share your food, everybody happy.' What does the song teach?
hints: What is the song telling us to do with food?
It makes everybody happy.
questions.explanation: The song teaches that sharing food makes everybody happy. Eating alone, singing loudly or running fast are not the lesson of this song.
questions.misconception: The lesson is the same as the actions in the song.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: Name one song that pupils sing at school assembly in Ghana.
hints: Think about the song for the whole country.
It is sung on Monday morning.
questions.explanation: The National Anthem (God Bless Our Homeland Ghana) is sung at school assembly. It is the song for the whole country.
questions.misconception: Any song can be sung at assembly.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: Which action fits a fast, happy song?
hints: Fast and happy means moving.
Use your hands and feet.
questions.explanation: A fast, happy song is sung with clapping and dancing. Sitting quietly, sleeping or crying fits slow or sad songs, not fast happy ones.
questions.misconception: Any action fits any song.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: A song says: 'Our school is green, our school is clean.' What is the song about?
hints: Listen to the word that is repeated.
It is where you learn.
questions.explanation: The song repeats 'our school' and describes it as green and clean. So the song is about the school, not the market, a farm or a bus.
questions.misconception: The song is about anything green.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: A song says: 'Pick up the rubbish, keep Ghana clean.' What lesson does this song teach?
options: We should keep our country clean
hints: What does the song ask us to do with rubbish?
It is about our country.
questions.explanation: The song teaches us to pick up rubbish so that Ghana stays clean. Throwing rubbish anywhere is the opposite of the lesson.
questions.misconception: The lesson is the same as naming who is in the song.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: At a naming ceremony in Ghana, which song is most suitable?
options: A welcome song for the baby
hints: The ceremony is for a new baby.
The song should welcome the baby.
questions.explanation: A naming ceremony welcomes a new baby, so a welcome song fits best. The National Anthem, a work song or a football chant do not fit a naming ceremony.
questions.misconception: Any song fits any occasion.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: Which action does NOT fit when singing a slow, quiet lullaby?
hints: A lullaby is for a baby to sleep.
It should be quiet and calm.
questions.explanation: Shouting and jumping do not fit a lullaby. A lullaby is sung softly, slowly and with gentle rocking so the baby can sleep.
questions.misconception: Loud is the same as expressive.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: A song says: 'Obey your parents, obey your teachers.' What does this song teach?
hints: Who does the song tell you to listen to?
The lesson is about doing what you are told.
questions.explanation: The song teaches obedience — we should obey our parents and our teachers. It is about listening and doing what we are told.
questions.misconception: The lesson is the same as naming the people in the song.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: Sing one familiar song you know. Use the right actions (clap, tap or dance) and sing with expression.

criteria.description: Sings the correct words of a familiar song
Uses at least one suitable action (clap, tap or dance)
Sings with appropriate expression (happy, soft, or solemn)

hints: Choose a song you know well.
Think about whether the song is happy, soft or solemn before you sing.
questions.explanation: This is a performance task. The teacher listens for correct words, suitable actions, matching expression and clear singing.
questions.misconception: Singing means only saying the words.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: Why is the National Anthem sung standing still and solemnly?
options: It is too long to dance to
It is a happy birthday song
It shows respect for the nation
It is a song for babies
hints: Think about what the anthem stands for.
It is not about the music — it is about the country.
questions.explanation: The National Anthem is sung standing still and solemnly to show respect for Ghana. It is not about the length of the song or dancing.
questions.misconception: The way we sing depends only on the tune.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: A song says: 'Work together, work together, we can build our nation.' The line is repeated many times. What does the repetition teach?
options: Singing is more important than working
hints: Why do you think the line is said again and again?
What does the line tell us to do?
questions.explanation: The line is repeated to make the lesson strong: working together is very important. It does not mean the song is too short or that one person should do all the work.
questions.misconception: Repetition is only for filling time.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: Sing the National Anthem with the correct words. Stand still and sing solemnly.

criteria.description: Sings the correct words of the National Anthem

hints: Remember the words you sing at assembly.
Stand straight and keep a serious face.
questions.explanation: This is a performance task. The teacher listens for correct words, standing still, a solemn expression and clear singing.
questions.misconception: The National Anthem can be sung like a play song.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and sing familiar songs with appropriate expressions

questions.stem: Ama says: 'Twinkle, twinkle, little star.' What is the name of this rhyme?
hints: The first two words of the rhyme are the same as the name.
It is about a star in the sky.
questions.explanation: The line 'Twinkle, twinkle, little star' is from the rhyme called Twinkle Twinkle Little Star. The other rhymes have different first lines.
questions.misconception: The first line does not tell the name of the rhyme.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: In the rhyme 'The cat sat on the mat', which word rhymes with 'cat'?
hints: Listen to the last sound of 'cat'.
'Mat' ends with the same sound as 'cat'.
questions.explanation: Cat and mat both end with the sound /at/. 'Sat' has the same ending but it is the verb in the line; the rhyming pair is cat–mat. 'Cot' and 'cut' end with different sounds.
questions.misconception: Words rhyme because they start with the same letter.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: In the rhyme 'Clap, clap, clap your hands', what action should you do?
hints: The words of the rhyme tell you what to do.
Look at the first word.
questions.explanation: The rhyme says 'Clap, clap, clap your hands', so the matching action is to clap your hands. Stamping, waving and nodding are different actions.
questions.misconception: Any action fits any line.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: The rhyme says: 'Rain, rain, go away.' What is the rhyme about?
hints: Look at the first word of the rhyme.
It falls from the sky.
questions.explanation: The rhyme talks about rain and asks it to go away. So the rhyme is about rain, not the sun, a dog or the moon.
questions.misconception: Rhymes have no meaning.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: Say 'She sells sea shells'. Which sound is repeated many times?
hints: Say the words slowly and listen.
The first sound of 'she' and 'shells'.
questions.explanation: The tongue-twister 'She sells sea shells' repeats the /s/ and /sh/ sounds. It does not repeat /m/, /b/ or /t/.
questions.misconception: A tongue-twister has no repeated sound.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: The rhyme goes: 'Baa, baa, black sheep, have you any wool?' Which rhyme is this?
hints: Look at the very first two words.
It is about a sheep.
questions.explanation: The line 'Baa, baa, black sheep' is from the rhyme Baa Baa Black Sheep. The other rhymes are about different characters.
questions.misconception: The first line does not tell you the rhyme.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: Which word rhymes with 'sun'?
hints: Listen to the last sound of 'sun'.
The rhyming word ends with the same sound /un/.
questions.explanation: Sun and run both end with /un/, so they rhyme. 'Son' sounds the same but is used differently in a rhyme. 'Sand' and 'sit' do not rhyme with 'sun'.
questions.misconception: Words rhyme because they start with the same letter.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: Which set of lines for 'Jack and Jill' is in the correct order?
options: Went up the hill / Jack and Jill / To fetch a pail of water
Jack and Jill / Went up the hill / To fetch a pail of water
To fetch a pail of water / Jack and Jill / Went up the hill
Jack and Jill / To fetch a pail of water / Went up the hill
hints: Who is the rhyme about?
What did they do first?
questions.explanation: The rhyme goes: Jack and Jill went up the hill to fetch a pail of water. The names come first, then the action, then the reason.
questions.misconception: Order does not matter in a rhyme.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: In the rhyme 'Row, row, row your boat', what action fits?
hints: What does 'row' mean?
It is done in a boat.
questions.explanation: The rhyme 'Row, row, row your boat' has the action of rowing a boat. You move your arms as if you are rowing. Jumping, clapping and stamping do not fit.
questions.misconception: Any action fits any rhyme.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: The rhyme says: 'Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall.' Where did Humpty Dumpty sit?
hints: Look at the words in the rhyme.
It is not inside a house.
questions.explanation: The rhyme says Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall. It does not say chair, table or mat. So the correct answer is 'on a wall'.
questions.misconception: Any place fits the rhyme.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: Say: 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled pepper.' Which sound is repeated many times?
hints: Look at the first letter of the main words.
Say the words slowly.
questions.explanation: The tongue-twister repeats the /p/ sound in 'Peter', 'Piper', 'picked', 'peck', 'pickled' and 'pepper'. It does not repeat /b/, /m/ or /t/.
questions.misconception: A tongue-twister has no repeated sound.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: Write one word that rhymes with 'hat'.
hints: Listen to the last sound of 'hat'.
Think of words ending in -at.
questions.explanation: Words that rhyme with 'hat' end with the same /at/ sound: cat, bat, mat, rat, fat, sat, pat. Any of these is correct.
questions.misconception: Words rhyme because they start with the same letter.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: The rhyme says: 'Hickory, dickory, dock, the mouse ran up the clock.' What did the mouse do?
hints: Read the last part of the line.
It is about a clock.
questions.explanation: The rhyme says the mouse ran up the clock. The other options are not in the rhyme. So the correct answer is 'ran up the clock'.
questions.misconception: Any action fits the rhyme.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: Which set of lines for 'Humpty Dumpty' is in the correct order?
options: Humpty Dumpty / Had a great fall / Sat on a wall
Sat on a wall / Humpty Dumpty / Had a great fall
Humpty Dumpty / Sat on a wall / Had a great fall
Had a great fall / Humpty Dumpty / Sat on a wall
hints: Who is the rhyme about?
What did Humpty Dumpty do first?
questions.explanation: The rhyme goes: Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall, Humpty Dumpty had a great fall. First he sits on the wall, then he falls. So the order is name, then sitting, then falling.
questions.misconception: Order does not matter in a rhyme.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: Which action does NOT fit the rhyme line 'Sleep, baby, sleep'?
hints: The line is about a baby sleeping.
It should be quiet and calm.
questions.explanation: The rhyme line 'Sleep, baby, sleep' is quiet and calm. Shouting and jumping do not fit; rocking, swaying and soft singing do. So the odd one out is shouting and jumping.
questions.misconception: Any action fits any line.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: Say the tongue-twister 'She sells sea shells' three times: first slowly and clearly, then faster, without mixing the words.

criteria.description: Says the tongue-twister slowly and clearly the first time
Says it faster without mixing the words

hints: Start slowly and say each word clearly.
Only go faster when you can say it without mixing the words.
questions.explanation: This is an oral performance task. The teacher listens for clear sounds at first, then growing speed without mistakes.
questions.misconception: A tongue-twister is only about speed.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: In the rhyme 'The cat sat on the mat', which TWO words rhyme?
hints: The question asks for two words that rhyme inside the line.
Look at the end of the line.
questions.explanation: The rhyme line pairs 'cat' and 'mat'. 'Sat' shares the /at/ ending, but the rhyme line 'cat sat on the mat' pairs the two nouns at the ends. So the rhyming pair is cat and mat.
questions.misconception: Rhyming means same meaning.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: Recite one short rhyme you know with the correct words and the right actions.

criteria.description: Uses matching actions for the rhyme

hints: Choose a rhyme you know well.
Plan the actions that match the words.
questions.explanation: This is a performance task. The teacher listens for a complete rhyme, correct words, matching actions and clear expression.
questions.misconception: Reciting means only saying the words.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: Say 'Red lorry, yellow lorry'. Which sound is repeated many times?
hints: Say the words slowly and listen.
Look at the middle of 'lorry'.
questions.explanation: The tongue-twister 'Red lorry, yellow lorry' repeats the /l/ sound in 'lorry', 'yellow' and 'lorry'. So the repeated sound is /l/.
questions.misconception: A tongue-twister has no repeated sound.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: Why is the rhyme 'Rain, rain, go away' often sung by children?
options: To stop the rain so they can play
hints: Why do children want the rain to go away?
They want to be outside.
questions.explanation: Children sing 'Rain, rain, go away' to ask the rain to stop so they can go outside and play. It is not about the sun, sleeping or animals.
questions.misconception: Rhymes have no meaning.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: Which line does NOT belong in the rhyme 'Twinkle, twinkle, little star'?
options: How I wonder what you are
Up above the world so high
The cow jumped over the moon
Like a diamond in the sky
hints: Which line is from a different rhyme?
One line mentions a cow and a moon.
questions.explanation: 'The cow jumped over the moon' belongs to the rhyme 'Hey Diddle Diddle', not to 'Twinkle, twinkle, little star'. The other three lines are all from the star rhyme.
questions.misconception: Order does not matter in a rhyme.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: Say 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled pepper' three times quickly without mixing the words.

criteria.description: Says all the words in the right order
Says the full tongue-twister three times without mixing the words

hints: Practise slowly first.
Say each /p/ sound clearly before going faster.
questions.explanation: This is an oral performance task. The teacher listens for all words in the right order, clear /p/ sounds, three full repetitions and increasing speed.
questions.misconception: A tongue-twister is only about speed, not clear words.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and recite rhymes and tongue-twisters with accompanying actions

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Ama has a small cat. The cat is black. Ama feeds the cat every day.' Who is in the story?
hints: Look for the names in the story.
One is a girl and one is an animal.
questions.explanation: The story names Ama and her cat. Kofi, the dog, the farmer, the cow, the teacher and the pupil are not in the story. So the characters are Ama and her cat.
questions.misconception: Any name fits the story.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Kwame has a goat. Kwame ties the goat to a tree. The goat eats grass.' What does Kwame do?
options: He ties the goat to a tree
hints: Find what Kwame does in the story.
It is about the goat and a tree.
questions.explanation: The story says Kwame ties the goat to a tree. The goat eats grass, not Kwame. Kwame does not sleep or run away.
questions.misconception: Role = name only.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Adjoa is a kind girl. She helps her mother in the house. She helps her father in the garden. Everybody loves Adjoa.' Who is the main character?
hints: Who is the story mostly about?
Whose name is repeated most?
questions.explanation: The story is mostly about Adjoa. Her name appears most often, and the story tells what she does. The mother, father and everybody are in the story but are not the main character.
questions.misconception: The first person mentioned is the main character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Kofi went to the market with his mother. He bought a mango. The seller smiled at him.' Who is a minor character?
hints: Who appears for just a small moment?
The story is mostly about Kofi.
questions.explanation: The seller appears only for a moment (she smiles) and the story is not about her. So she is a minor character. The market and mango are not characters.
questions.misconception: Any named person is the main character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Mother said, "Ama, come and eat." Ama said, "Thank you, Mother."' Who said 'Thank you, Mother'?
hints: Look for the line in the story.
Who is saying it back to the mother?
questions.explanation: Ama says 'Thank you, Mother.' Mother says 'Ama, come and eat.' So the correct answer is Ama.
questions.misconception: The narrator is a character who says the lines.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'The sun was hot. Kofi and Ama walked to school. A dog followed them. The dog was friendly.' Which animals are in the story?
hints: Listen for the animal.
The animal follows Kofi and Ama.
questions.explanation: The story says a dog followed them. There is no cat, goat or cow in the story. So the correct answer is a dog.
questions.misconception: Any animal fits the story.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Abena has a small brother. His name is Kojo. Kojo cries a lot. Abena sings to him. Kojo stops crying and sleeps.' What does Abena do?
hints: Find what Abena does to help.
It stops Kojo from crying.
questions.explanation: Abena sings to Kojo. Kojo cries and sleeps, not Abena. She does not eat food in the story. So her role is to sing to her brother.
questions.misconception: Role = the other character's action.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'A big lion lived in the forest. One day the lion could not find food. He walked and walked. He saw a small ant. The ant was too small to eat. The lion sat down and cried.' Who is the main character?
hints: Who is the story mostly about?
Whose name is said most?
questions.explanation: The story is mostly about the lion — it tells what the lion did and how he felt. The ant appears only at the end. The forest is a setting, not a character.
questions.misconception: The last character mentioned is the main character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Yaa said, "I want water." Her mother said, "Here is some water." Yaa drank the water.' Who wanted water?
hints: Look at the first quotation.
It is the child in the story.
questions.explanation: Yaa says 'I want water.' So Yaa wanted water. Her mother gives it to her, but her mother did not ask for water.
questions.misconception: The person giving the item is the one who wanted it.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads a short story. Then answer: who is in the story, and what does one character do?

criteria.description: Names at least one character in the story
Listens quietly while the story is read

hints: Listen carefully for names.
Think about what each character does.
questions.explanation: This is a listening task. The teacher reads a short story, then listens for the pupil to name a character and say what they do.
questions.misconception: Listening is the same as reading.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Musa went to the farm. He planted maize. His sister Fatima came to help. A bird sang in a tree nearby.' Who is a minor character?
hints: Which character appears only for a small moment?
The story is mostly about Musa.
questions.explanation: The bird appears only once, singing in a tree. Fatima comes to help Musa and is part of the action, but the bird is a minor character with a small part. Maize is not a character.
questions.misconception: Anyone mentioned is the main character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Read: 'Ekua has a pet rabbit. The rabbit is white. Ekua feeds the rabbit with carrots.' Name the characters in the story.
hints: Look for names and animals.
One is a girl and one is a small animal.
questions.explanation: The characters are Ekua and her rabbit. Both are named or described in the story. Carrots are not a character.
questions.misconception: Only the first character counts.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Kojo lost his pencil. He looked under the table. He looked in his bag. Ama said, "Here is your pencil. It fell near the door." Kojo was happy.' What is Ama's role in the story?
options: She helps Kojo find his pencil
hints: What does Ama say to Kojo?
Her words give Kojo the answer.
questions.explanation: Ama tells Kojo where his pencil is, so she helps him find it. Kojo is the one who loses the pencil and looks under the table. The story does not say Ama is a teacher.
questions.misconception: Role = name only.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'The teacher said, "Open your books." Kofi opened his book. Ama could not find her book. She said, "Teacher, I cannot find my book."' Who said 'Teacher, I cannot find my book'?
hints: Which pupil could not find a book?
Kofi opened his book — he was not the one speaking.
questions.explanation: Ama could not find her book, so Ama says those words. Kofi opened his book. The teacher gives the instruction, not the reply.
questions.misconception: The teacher says all the lines in a class story.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'There was a big fire in the forest. All the animals ran away. The rabbit did not run. The rabbit ran to the river. It carried water in a small leaf. It tried to put out the fire. The elephant saw the rabbit and helped.' Who is the main character?
hints: Who does most of the actions in the story?
The elephant only appears at the end.
questions.explanation: The rabbit is in almost every sentence — it does not run, it goes to the river, it carries water, it tries to put out the fire. The elephant appears only at the end. So the rabbit is the main character.
questions.misconception: The biggest animal is the main character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Mr Mensah is a teacher. He teaches English in a school. His class has twenty pupils. One pupil is Adjoa. She loves reading. A visitor came to watch the class. Mr Mensah greeted the visitor.' Who is a minor character?
hints: Which person appears only once and does not do much?
The story is about Mr Mensah and his class.
questions.explanation: The visitor comes to watch and is greeted — they appear once at the end and have only one small action. Mr Mensah and Adjoa are more important to the story. The class is not a character.
questions.misconception: Anyone mentioned is a main character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads a short story. Then answer: who is the main character, who is a minor character, and what does each one do?

criteria.description: Says what the main character does
Says what the minor character does

hints: Listen for who the story is mostly about.
Also listen for someone who only appears briefly.
questions.explanation: This is a listening task. The teacher reads a short story and listens for the pupil to identify both a main and a minor character with their roles.
questions.misconception: All characters are equally important.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'In a small village lived an old woman named Maame Adwoa. She sold oranges at the market. Every day, a boy named Yaw bought two oranges. One day, Yaw did not come. Maame Adwoa asked about him. She learned that Yaw was sick. She took oranges to Yaw's house. Yaw's mother thanked her.' Who is NOT a character in the story?
hints: A character is a person (or animal) who does something in the story.
A place is not a character.
questions.explanation: The market is a place (a setting), not a character. Maame Adwoa, Yaw and Yaw's mother all do or say something in the story. So the market is not a character.
questions.misconception: Characters and setting are the same.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Kwesi and his sister Ama went to the river. Kwesi slipped and fell into the water. Ama shouted for help. A fisherman heard her. He pulled Kwesi out. The fisherman gave Kwesi a dry cloth. Ama thanked the fisherman. The fisherman said, "Take care near the water." The two children went home.' Who is the main character?
hints: Who has the problem in the story?
The story is about what happens to him.
questions.explanation: The story is centred on Kwesi's problem — he falls into the water and needs help. Ama, the fisherman and the river are all part of the story, but the story is mostly about Kwesi.
questions.misconception: The one who does the most actions is always the main character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads a short story with a conversation. Then say which character said each of two lines: 'Take care near the water' and 'Thank you, sir.'

criteria.description: Correctly names who said 'Take care near the water'
Correctly names who said 'Thank you, sir'
Explains why that character said the line

hints: Listen for who gives advice and who gives thanks.
Who would say 'Thank you' in a story like this?
questions.explanation: This is a listening task. The teacher reads a short story with a conversation and listens for the pupil to identify the speakers correctly and give a simple reason.
questions.misconception: The narrator says all lines.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to stories and be able to identify characters with their roles

questions.stem: Read this story: 'Ama woke up early. She washed her face. She ate her food. She went to school.' How did the story begin?
hints: What happened first in the story?
It is the very first thing Ama did.
questions.explanation: The story begins with 'Ama woke up early.' Washing, eating and going to school happen after she wakes up. So the beginning is 'Ama woke up early.'
questions.misconception: The last action is the beginning.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read this story: 'Kofi found a mango. He washed it. He ate it.' How did the story end?
hints: What is the last thing Kofi did?
It comes after washing.
questions.explanation: The last thing Kofi does in the story is eat the mango. Finding and washing come first. Sleeping is not in the story.
questions.misconception: The first thing is the ending.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read this story: 'The sun was hot. Ama took her umbrella. She walked to the market. She bought rice.' How did the story begin?
hints: What is the first sentence of the story?
It is about the weather.
questions.explanation: The first sentence says 'The sun was hot.' The other events happen after. So the beginning is 'The sun was hot.'
questions.misconception: The most important event comes first.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read this story: 'Ama woke up. She ate her food. She went to school.' What happened in the middle?
hints: What comes between waking up and going to school?
It is something she ate.
questions.explanation: The order is: woke up, ate her food, went to school. So the middle event is 'She ate her food.' Waking up is the start and going to school is the end.
questions.misconception: The middle is the start.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read: 'Kwame washed his hands. He sat at the table. He ate his lunch.' How did the story end?
hints: What is the last action in the story?
It is something to do with food.
questions.explanation: The last action in the story is Kwame eating his lunch. Washing his hands and sitting at the table happen before.
questions.misconception: The first action is the ending.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read this story: 'Ama woke up. She washed her face. She went to school.' Which order is correct?
options: Washed her face → Woke up → Went to school
Went to school → Woke up → Washed her face
Ama woke up → Washed her face → Went to school
Ama woke up → Went to school → Washed her face
hints: What is the first thing Ama did?
Washing comes before going to school.
questions.explanation: The story order is: she woke up, then washed her face, then went to school. Only option 3 follows that order.
questions.misconception: Order does not matter in a retell.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read this story: 'Ama had a red bag. She put her books inside. She walked to school. On the way, she lost the bag. A teacher found it and gave it back to her.' Which is the KEY event that must be in a retell?
hints: Which event changes the story?
It causes a problem for Ama.
questions.explanation: Losing the bag is the key event — it creates the problem that the teacher later solves. The bag being red or having books inside are small details. The teacher being tall is not even in the story.
questions.misconception: Small details are the key event.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read this story: 'Kofi went to the market. He bought a mango. He ate the mango. He went home.' Which order is correct?
options: Went to market → Ate the mango → Bought the mango → Went home
Went to market → Bought the mango → Ate the mango → Went home
Went home → Went to market → Bought the mango → Ate the mango
Bought the mango → Went to market → Ate the mango → Went home
hints: What did Kofi do first?
He must buy the mango before he eats it.
questions.explanation: Kofi goes to the market first, then buys a mango, then eats it, then goes home. He cannot eat before buying. Only option 2 follows this order.
questions.misconception: Order does not matter.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read this story: 'Ama found a small bird. The bird had a hurt wing. Ama put the bird in a box. She gave it food and water. The bird got well and flew away.' Which picture best matches the MIDDLE of the story?
options: A bird flying high in the sky
Ama holding a box with the bird inside
Ama waking up in the morning
hints: What happens in the middle?
Ama takes care of the bird.
questions.explanation: The middle of the story is when Ama cares for the bird in the box. A flying bird is the end. Waking up and running to school are not in the story.
questions.misconception: Pictures are decorative.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read this story: 'Kofi found a coin on the road. He picked it up. He put it in his pocket. He bought sweets with it. He shared the sweets with his sister.' How did the story end?
options: Kofi shared sweets with his sister
Kofi put the coin in his pocket
hints: What is the last thing that happened?
It involves his sister.
questions.explanation: The last action in the story is Kofi sharing the sweets with his sister. Finding the coin, picking it up and putting it in the pocket happen before.
questions.misconception: The start is the ending.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read this story: 'Ama went to the river to fetch water. The pot was heavy. She rested under a tree. A kind woman helped her carry the pot. Ama thanked her.' Which is the KEY event?
options: The kind woman helped Ama carry the pot
hints: Which event solves Ama's problem?
The pot was heavy.
questions.explanation: Ama's problem is the heavy pot. The key event is when the kind woman helps her carry it. Resting and thanking are smaller parts of the story.
questions.misconception: The first event is the key event.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read this story: 'Kofi washed his hands. He sat at the table. He ate his food.' Write the middle event.
hints: What comes between washing hands and eating food?
It involves a table.
questions.explanation: The order is: washed his hands, sat at the table, ate his food. The middle event is 'He sat at the table.'
questions.misconception: The middle is the first event.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read this story: 'It was a hot afternoon. Ama was walking home from school. She saw an old man carrying a heavy bag. Ama helped the old man. The old man gave her a sweet. Ama walked home happily.' How did the story begin?
options: The old man gave her a sweet
hints: Which sentence comes first in the story?
It describes the weather.
questions.explanation: The very first sentence is 'It was a hot afternoon.' Everything else comes after. So the beginning is 'It was a hot afternoon.'
questions.misconception: The most interesting part is the beginning.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read this story: 'Kwame woke up late. He could not find his uniform. His mother helped him look. The uniform was under the bed. Kwame dressed quickly and ran to school.' Which picture best matches the BEGINNING of the story?
options: Kwame and his mother finding the uniform
hints: What is the very first thing that happens?
It involves waking up.
questions.explanation: The story begins with Kwame waking up late. Running to school is the end. Finding the uniform is in the middle. Wearing the uniform is also near the end.
questions.misconception: Pictures do not need to match the order.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read this story: 'The rain started. Ama ran home. She was wet. She changed her clothes.' Which order is correct?
options: The rain started → She changed her clothes → She was wet → Ama ran home
The rain started → Ama ran home → She was wet → She changed her clothes
Ama ran home → The rain started → She was wet → She changed her clothes
She changed her clothes → The rain started → Ama ran home → She was wet
hints: The rain comes first.
She can only change her clothes after she is wet.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: rain starts, Ama runs home, she is wet, she changes her clothes. Only option 2 follows this.
questions.misconception: Order does not matter.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read this story: 'The class went to the zoo. They saw a big lion. Ama was afraid. Kofi held her hand. The class went home.' What happened in the MIDDLE of the story?
options: The class went to the zoo
Ama was afraid and Kofi held her hand
hints: What happened after they saw the lion but before they went home?
Ama was scared.
questions.explanation: The middle of the story is when Ama was afraid and Kofi held her hand. Going to the zoo is the beginning, going home is the end, and no elephant is mentioned.
questions.misconception: The middle is the beginning.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads a short story. Then retell the story in the correct order, using the pictures your teacher shows you.

criteria.description: Retells the story in the correct order (beginning, middle, end)
Uses own words (not just repeating exactly)

hints: Look at the pictures in order.
Say the beginning, then the middle, then the end.
questions.explanation: This is an oral retelling task. The teacher listens for correct order, the key event, own words and a clear voice.
questions.misconception: Retelling means saying every word from memory.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads a story with a problem and a solution. Retell the story, making sure to say what the problem was and how it was solved.

criteria.description: Retells the beginning of the story
Explains how the problem was solved

hints: Listen for what went wrong.
Think about who solved the problem.
questions.explanation: This is an extended oral retelling task. The teacher listens for beginning, problem, solution and ending all in order.
questions.misconception: A retell can stop after the problem.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Tell a short story that you know well from your family or community, in the correct order. Include a beginning, a middle and an end.

criteria.description: Tells a story the pupil knows
Beginning, middle and end are all present
Story is told in a logical order

hints: Choose a story you have heard at home.
Think about how it starts, what happens and how it ends.
questions.explanation: This is a performance task. The teacher listens for a complete story in logical order and a confident, clear voice.
questions.misconception: Only stories from books can be retold.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Retell a short story you know. At the exciting part, pause for the class to sing a short song that fits the story, then continue to the end.

criteria.description: Pauses at a suitable moment for the song
Continues the story after the song
Uses a clear voice and engaging expression

hints: Pause where something exciting happens.
Choose a song the class knows that fits the story.
questions.explanation: This is an extended oral performance task. The teacher listens for a well-ordered retell, a suitable pause for the song and a strong finish.
questions.misconception: The song comes at the very end, not in the middle.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell short stories

questions.stem: Read this story: 'Ama had a small bird. The bird had a hurt wing. Ama put the bird in a box. She gave it food. The bird got well and flew away.' Which characters are in the story?
hints: Look for the names and animals in the story.
One is a girl and one is a small animal with wings.
questions.explanation: The story is about Ama and the bird. Kofi, the goat, the farmer, the cow, the teacher and the pupil are not in this story. So the characters are Ama and the bird.
questions.misconception: Any name fits the story.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: In the story 'Ama and the bird', Ama puts the bird in a box and gives it food. What action should the pupil playing Ama do?
options: Pretend to put something in a box and give food
Pretend to fly high in the sky
hints: What does Ama do in the story?
She helps the bird.
questions.explanation: Ama's actions in the story are putting the bird in a box and giving it food. Flying, eating grass and sleeping are not Ama's actions. So the correct action is to pretend to put something in a box and give food.
questions.misconception: Any action fits any character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: In a drama of 'Ama and the bird', which pupil should play the character who has a hurt wing?
options: The pupil who plays the bird
The pupil who plays the box
The pupil who plays the food
hints: Which character has a hurt wing?
It is the small animal.
questions.explanation: The bird is the character with a hurt wing. Ama is the girl who helps, and the box and food are objects, not characters. So the pupil playing the bird should play that character.
questions.misconception: Any pupil can play any role, regardless of the character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: How should the pupil playing the bird speak when it is hurt?
hints: The bird is hurt.
It is small and needs help.
questions.explanation: A hurt bird would speak softly and weakly, not loudly or happily. The pupil playing the bird should use a soft, weak voice to show the bird is hurt.
questions.misconception: Any voice fits any character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: Read this story: 'Kofi had a goat. The goat ate Kofi's book. Kofi was sad.' Name the characters in the story.
hints: Who is the story about?
One is a boy and one is an animal.
questions.explanation: The characters are Kofi and his goat. Both are named in the story. The book is an object, not a character.
questions.misconception: Only the first character counts.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: In a drama, a pupil is playing a greedy character who takes all the food. Which action fits this character?
hints: What does 'greedy' mean?
Greedy people take more than they need.
questions.explanation: A greedy character grabs food and hides it instead of sharing. Sharing, cooking for others and serving politely are actions of a kind character, not a greedy one.
questions.misconception: A character's actions can be anything.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: In a drama of 'The Lion and the Ant', the story says: 'The lion was big and proud. The ant was small and brave.' Which pupil should play the ant?
options: The pupil who can roar loudly
A pupil who is small and speaks bravely
A pupil who is good at sleeping
hints: The ant is small and brave.
Match the pupil to the character's description.
questions.explanation: The ant is described as small and brave, so a pupil who is small and can speak bravely fits the ant. The tallest pupil or one who roars loudly would fit the lion better. Sleeping does not match the ant.
questions.misconception: Any pupil can play any role.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: A pupil is playing a kind old woman who helps a child. How should she speak?
hints: The character is kind.
She is helping a child.
questions.explanation: A kind old woman who helps a child would speak softly and kindly. Angry, cross or baby voices do not fit her character.
questions.misconception: Any voice fits any character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: In the drama 'Kofi and the Goat', which scene should come FIRST?
hints: What must happen before the goat can eat the book?
Kofi must have a goat first.
questions.explanation: Kofi must get the goat before the goat can eat his book. So 'Kofi gets a goat' comes first. The goat eating the book, Kofi being sad and his mother scolding the goat all come later.
questions.misconception: Scene order does not matter.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: A pupil is pretending to look under a bed and pull out a uniform. Which scene from the story 'Kwame is Late' is being acted?
hints: What is the pupil looking for?
It is the missing uniform.
questions.explanation: Looking under the bed and pulling out a uniform shows the scene where Kwame finds his uniform. Waking up, running to school and eating breakfast involve different actions.
questions.misconception: Pictures and clues do not match a scene.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: In a group, role-play the character Ama from 'Ama and the bird'. Show the class how Ama puts the bird in a box and feeds it. Use words and actions that fit Ama.

criteria.description: Stays in the role of Ama throughout
Uses actions that match the story (box, feeding)
Works with the group without grabbing others' parts

hints: Think about how Ama would move and speak.
Show kindness in your actions.
questions.explanation: This is a performance task. The teacher watches for staying in role, matching actions, a kind voice and group cooperation.
questions.misconception: Acting means only saying lines.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: In a group of three, act out the beginning of the story 'The Kind Woman'. One pupil plays Ama, one plays the old woman and one plays the narrator. Act the scene where Ama helps the old woman carry the heavy pot.

criteria.description: Each pupil stays in their role
Actions match the story (carrying the pot, helping)
The group works together in order

hints: Think about what each character would say and do.
The narrator tells the story between the acting.
questions.explanation: This is a group performance task. The teacher watches for each pupil staying in role, matching actions and voices, and the group working together in the right order.
questions.misconception: One person can do all the parts.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: In the drama 'The Lost Bag', a pupil is acting out these scenes. Which order is correct?
options: Teacher finds the bag → Ama loses the bag → Ama thanks the teacher → Ama walks to school
Ama walks to school → Ama loses the bag → Teacher finds the bag → Ama thanks the teacher
Ama loses the bag → Ama walks to school → Ama thanks the teacher → Teacher finds the bag
Ama thanks the teacher → Ama loses the bag → Teacher finds the bag → Ama walks to school
hints: Ama must lose the bag before it can be found.
She must be on her way to school first.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: Ama walks to school, Ama loses the bag, the teacher finds it, Ama thanks the teacher. Only option 2 follows this order.
questions.misconception: Scene order does not matter in a drama.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: A pupil is pretending to cry and look at a broken pot on the ground. Which scene from the story 'Ama Breaks the Pot' is being acted?
options: Ama fetching water from the river
Ama dropping and breaking the pot
Ama telling her mother what happened
hints: The pot is broken on the ground.
What happened just before the crying?
questions.explanation: Crying and looking at a broken pot shows the scene where Ama drops and breaks the pot. Fetching water, carrying the pot and telling her mother involve different actions.
questions.misconception: Any scene can be acted with any action.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: After the drama, tell the class: what role did you play, and what did your character do in the story?

criteria.description: Speaks clearly and looks at the audience

hints: Think about what your character did in the story.
Speak clearly so everyone can hear.
questions.explanation: This is an oral reflection task. The teacher listens for the pupil to name their role, describe what the character did and speak clearly.
questions.misconception: Talking about roles is not part of drama.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: In your group, act out a short scene from 'Kofi and the Goat'. Show that you can work together: take turns, listen to each other and do not grab anyone's part.

criteria.description: Does not grab or interrupt others' parts
Stays with the group until the scene ends

hints: Wait for your turn before you act.
Listen when your partner is acting.
questions.explanation: This is a practical group task. The teacher watches for turn-taking, listening, not interrupting and staying with the group.
questions.misconception: Grabbing lines shows you are a good actor.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: In a group of four, act out the whole story of 'The Lion and the Ant'. One plays the lion, one plays the ant, one plays the narrator and one plays the other animals. Use actions and voices that match each character.

criteria.description: Each pupil stays in role for the whole scene
Actions match the story and the character
Voices match the character (loud/proud lion, small/brave ant)
The group follows the scene order correctly

hints: The lion is big and proud, so speak loudly and stand tall.
The ant is small and brave, so speak bravely but not loudly.
questions.explanation: This is a group performance task. The teacher watches for staying in role, matching actions and voices, and correct scene order.
questions.misconception: All characters can use the same voice.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: In a group, act out a scene where two characters disagree and then make up. Show clear differences in the way each character speaks and acts. End the scene with the characters shaking hands or saying sorry.

criteria.description: Both characters stay in role throughout
Shows a clear difference between the two characters (voice and actions)
The scene ends with making up (handshake or apology)

hints: Think about what each character wants.
Show the change from disagreeing to making up.
questions.explanation: This is an extended performance task. The teacher watches for clear character differences, a clear disagreement and a clear resolution.
questions.misconception: Acting means just saying lines without showing feelings.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: After the drama, answer these questions: (1) What was your role? (2) What did you do well? (3) What did your partner do well? (4) What would you change if you acted it again?

criteria.description: Says one thing they did well
Says one thing their partner did well
Suggests one improvement for next time

hints: Think about what went well and what could be better.
Be kind when you talk about your partner.
questions.explanation: This is an extended oral reflection task. The teacher listens for the pupil to name their role, reflect on their own work, praise their partner and suggest an improvement.
questions.misconception: Only the acting matters, not the reflection.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: Plan and perform a short drama with your group. During the planning, show good teamwork: share ideas, agree on roles and make sure everyone has a turn to speak.

criteria.description: Makes sure everyone gets a speaking part

hints: Listen to everyone's idea before deciding.
Make sure shy pupils also get a turn.
questions.explanation: This is a practical group task. The teacher watches for sharing ideas, fair role allocation, including everyone and peaceful problem-solving.
questions.misconception: The group leader should do all the talking.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Dramatise stories heard

questions.stem: It is 7 o'clock in the morning. You meet your teacher at the school gate. What do you say?
hints: What time of day is 7 o'clock in the morning?
The sun is just rising.
questions.explanation: At 7 o'clock in the morning, the correct greeting is 'Good morning'. 'Good afternoon' is for the afternoon, 'Good evening' is for the evening and 'Good night' is said at bedtime.
questions.misconception: 'Good night' is an evening greeting.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: Your friend says 'Good morning' to you. What do you say back?
hints: How do you answer a greeting?
You give the same greeting back.
questions.explanation: When someone says 'Good morning' to you, you reply 'Good morning'. 'Good night' is for bedtime, 'Thank you' is for something given and 'Please' is for a request.
questions.misconception: 'Good morning' is a response, not a greeting.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: It is 2 o'clock in the afternoon. You meet your neighbour. What do you say?
hints: It is after 12 o'clock.
It is not yet evening.
questions.explanation: At 2 o'clock in the afternoon, the correct greeting is 'Good afternoon'. Morning is before 12 o'clock, evening is later in the day and 'Good night' is for bedtime.
questions.misconception: Any greeting works at any time.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: You see a picture of the sun setting. What greeting fits this time?
hints: The sun is going down.
It is the end of the day but not bedtime yet.
questions.explanation: When the sun is setting, it is evening. The correct greeting is 'Good evening'. 'Good night' is said when going to bed, and morning and afternoon are earlier in the day.
questions.misconception: 'Good night' is an evening greeting.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: Your teacher says 'Good afternoon, Ama.' What should Ama say?
hints: What greeting did the teacher give?
Reply with the same greeting.
questions.explanation: The teacher said 'Good afternoon', so Ama should reply 'Good afternoon, teacher'. It is polite to return the same greeting.
questions.misconception: You can reply with any greeting.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: Which of these is a polite greeting?
hints: A greeting is a kind word when you meet someone.
It shows respect.
questions.explanation: 'Good evening, sir' is a polite greeting. The other options are commands or rude remarks, not greetings. Greetings are polite words we use when we meet someone.
questions.misconception: Greeting is the same as saying goodbye.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: Ama is on her way to school in the morning. She meets her friend Kofi. Which greeting is best?
hints: It is morning.
She is greeting him, not saying goodbye.
questions.explanation: In the morning, the correct greeting is 'Good morning'. 'Good night' is for bedtime, 'Good evening' is for later in the day and 'Goodbye' is used when leaving, not when meeting.
questions.misconception: Greeting is the same as saying goodbye.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: At 7 o'clock in the evening, Papa returns from work. What does his child say?
hints: It is 7 o'clock in the evening.
The sun has gone down.
questions.explanation: At 7 o'clock in the evening, the correct greeting is 'Good evening'. Morning and afternoon are earlier in the day, and 'Goodbye' is used when leaving.
questions.misconception: 'Good night' is an evening greeting.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: Someone says 'Good night' to you as you go to bed. What is the correct response?
hints: Reply with the same words.
This is the bedtime greeting.
questions.explanation: When someone says 'Good night' as you go to bed, you reply 'Good night'. The other greetings are for other times of the day.
questions.misconception: 'Good night' is not a bedtime greeting.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: Why do we greet people?
hints: Greetings are polite words.
They show how we feel about others.
questions.explanation: We greet people to show respect and friendliness. Greetings are not for showing anger, making people go away or asking for money. They help us build good relationships.
questions.misconception: Only adults greet.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: You see a picture of the sun high in the sky at midday. What greeting fits this time?
hints: The sun is high in the sky at midday.
It is after 12 o'clock.
questions.explanation: When the sun is high in the sky at midday, it is afternoon. The correct greeting is 'Good afternoon'. Morning is before 12 o'clock and evening is later in the day.
questions.misconception: Any greeting works at any time.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: Why do we greet our teachers and friends?
hints: It is a way of being kind.
It shows you value the person.
questions.explanation: We greet our teachers and friends to show respect and to be polite. Greetings help us build good relationships with people around us.
questions.misconception: Greetings are not important.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: Ama's mother is leaving for work at 8 o'clock in the morning. Ama says 'Good morning, Mama.' Her mother replies 'Good morning, Ama. Have a nice day!' Is this the right greeting?
hints: What time is 8 o'clock?
Morning is before 12 o'clock.
questions.explanation: 8 o'clock in the morning is in the morning, so 'Good morning' is the correct greeting. 'Good night' is for bedtime and 'Good afternoon' is for after 12 o'clock. 'Goodbye' is said when leaving but the greeting itself is 'Good morning'.
questions.misconception: Any greeting works at any time.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: Greet your partner with a morning greeting. Your partner will reply. Then swap roles and do it again.

criteria.description: Uses the correct morning greeting ('Good morning')
Uses a polite voice and looks at partner

hints: Use 'Good morning'.
Look at your partner and smile.
questions.explanation: This is an oral pair task. The teacher listens for the correct morning greeting, a polite voice and eye contact, and an appropriate reply.
questions.misconception: Greeting is the same as saying goodbye.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: Greet your partner with an afternoon greeting. Then respond when your partner greets you.

criteria.description: Uses the correct afternoon greeting ('Good afternoon')

hints: Use 'Good afternoon'.
Reply with the same greeting.
questions.explanation: This is an oral pair task. The teacher listens for the correct afternoon greeting and a polite reply.
questions.misconception: Any greeting works at any time.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: Kofi greets his neighbour every morning. His neighbour always smiles and greets him back. What does this show?
hints: The neighbour smiles.
They greet each other every day.
questions.explanation: When Kofi greets his neighbour and she smiles and greets him back, it shows that greetings build good friendship. Greetings do not make people angry; they are for everyone, children included.
questions.misconception: Only adults greet.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: A pupil meets the head teacher in the corridor. Which greeting is the most polite?
hints: The head teacher is an adult in a position of respect.
Use a respectful greeting.
questions.explanation: 'Good morning, sir' is the most polite greeting for the head teacher. 'Hey!', 'Hi there' and 'What do you want?' are informal or rude and do not show respect.
questions.misconception: Any greeting is acceptable for any person.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: In pairs, act out this scene: one pupil is greeting a visitor at school at 3 o'clock in the afternoon. Greet the visitor politely, respond to their greeting, and say goodbye at the end of the visit.

criteria.description: Uses the correct afternoon greeting ('Good afternoon')
Responds appropriately to the visitor's greeting
Says goodbye correctly at the end

hints: It is the afternoon.
Use 'Good afternoon' to greet and 'Goodbye' when the visitor leaves.
questions.explanation: This is an oral pair role-play. The teacher listens for the correct afternoon greeting, polite speech, a good reply and a correct goodbye.
questions.misconception: Greeting and goodbye are the same thing.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: Which of these is the BEST reason to greet someone?
options: Because it is a rule and you will be punished
Because it makes the other person feel respected and valued
Because you want them to give you something
Because everyone else is doing it
hints: Greetings should be genuine.
Think about how a greeting makes the other person feel.
questions.explanation: The best reason to greet someone is that it makes the other person feel respected and valued. Greeting because of a rule, to get something or because everyone else is doing it is not genuine respect.
questions.misconception: Only adults greet.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: In pairs, act out a short conversation where you greet each other in the morning, ask each other 'How are you?', answer, and then say goodbye because you are going to class.

criteria.description: Asks 'How are you?' and answers appropriately

hints: Start with 'Good morning'.
After greeting, ask 'How are you?' and answer when you are asked.
questions.explanation: This is an extended oral pair task. The teacher listens for the morning greeting, the 'How are you?' exchange, a polite goodbye and clear speaking.
questions.misconception: Greeting is the same as saying goodbye.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Use appropriate greetings for different times of the day

questions.stem: Which of these is a room in a home?
hints: Think about rooms inside a house.
It is where food is cooked.
questions.explanation: A kitchen is a room inside a home. A market, a classroom and a church are places outside the home. Other rooms in a home include the bedroom, sitting room and bathroom.
questions.misconception: A home is only a building, not rooms inside.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe the home, people or places

questions.stem: Who is the person who teaches you at school?
hints: This person works in a classroom.
You see them every school day.
questions.explanation: A teacher is the person who teaches pupils at school. A farmer works on a farm, a doctor treats sick people and a driver drives a vehicle.
questions.misconception: Any adult is a teacher.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe the home, people or places

questions.stem: Which place is for buying and selling food and other things?
hints: People go there to buy things.
It is often busy and noisy.
questions.explanation: A market is where people buy and sell food and other goods. A school is for learning, a hospital is for sick people and a church is for worship.
questions.misconception: Place names are descriptions.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe the home, people or places

questions.stem: My house is very ______. It has many rooms. Which word fits best?
hints: The house has many rooms.
Which word describes the size of a house?
questions.explanation: A house with many rooms is 'big'. 'Sweet' and 'tasty' describe food, and 'loud' describes sound. So 'big' is the right describing word for a house.
questions.misconception: Any adjective fits any noun.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe the home, people or places

questions.stem: Name one room in a home where people sleep.
hints: It has a bed in it.
It is where you sleep at night.
questions.explanation: The bedroom is the room in a home where people sleep. It usually has a bed and other things for sleeping.
questions.misconception: Any room is a bedroom.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe the home, people or places

questions.stem: My father is a ______ man. He helps everybody. Which word fits best?
hints: The sentence says 'He helps everybody.'
What kind of person helps everyone?
questions.explanation: A man who helps everybody is 'kind'. 'Tall', 'noisy' and 'fast' do not describe being helpful. So 'kind' is the best fit.
questions.misconception: Any adjective fits any noun.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe the home, people or places

questions.stem: Ama is my friend. She is ______ and she has short hair. Which word fits?
hints: The sentence is about a person's appearance.
It is the opposite of 'short'.
questions.explanation: When describing a person's height, we say 'tall' or 'short'. 'Sour' and 'wet' describe food or water, and 'loud' describes sound. So 'tall' fits best.
questions.misconception: Any adjective fits any person.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe the home, people or places

questions.stem: The market near my house is very ______. There are many people and many stalls. Which word fits?
hints: There are many people and stalls.
It is not quiet or empty.
questions.explanation: A market with many people and stalls is 'busy'. 'Quiet' and 'empty' mean the opposite. 'Cold' describes the weather, not how busy a place is.
questions.misconception: Any adjective fits any place.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe the home, people or places

questions.stem: Which sentence BEST describes a home?
options: My home is a house with three rooms.
hints: The best description gives details.
It should say something about the home.
questions.explanation: 'My home is a house with three rooms' gives a clear description with a detail. The other options only name the home without describing it.
questions.misconception: One word is a full description.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe the home, people or places

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher describes a person: 'This person is tall. She wears a white coat. She helps sick people.' Which person is the teacher describing?

criteria.description: Names the correct person (a nurse or doctor)
Explains why (white coat, helps sick people)
Listens quietly while the teacher describes

hints: Listen for what the person wears.
Listen for what the person does.
questions.explanation: This is a listening task. The teacher describes a person and the pupil listens for clues: a white coat and helping sick people point to a nurse or doctor.
questions.misconception: Listening is the same as reading.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe the home, people or places

questions.stem: Describe your home in two simple sentences. Say what kind of home it is and one thing about it.

criteria.description: Says what kind of home it is (a house, a flat, etc.)
Gives one detail about the home (colour, size, rooms)

hints: Start with 'My home is...'
Then add one detail: 'It is big' or 'It has four rooms.'
questions.explanation: This is an oral description task. The teacher listens for two sentences, one identifying the home and one giving a detail, spoken clearly.
questions.misconception: Describe means only name.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe the home, people or places

questions.stem: Describe a person in your family in two simple sentences. Say who they are and one thing about them.

criteria.description: Names who the person is (mother, father, sister)
Gives one detail (tall, kind, works as...)

hints: Start with 'My mother is...'
Add a detail like 'She is kind' or 'She is a teacher.'
questions.explanation: This is an oral description task. The teacher listens for the person's identity, a detail and two clear sentences.
questions.misconception: One word is a full description.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe the home, people or places

questions.stem: Describe a place in your community in two or three simple sentences. Say what the place is and two things about it.

criteria.description: Gives at least one detail about the place

hints: Start with 'The market is...'
Add details: 'It is big' and 'It is busy.'
questions.explanation: This is an oral description task. The teacher listens for the place name, at least one detail and clear, complete sentences.
questions.misconception: Place names are descriptions.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe the home, people or places

questions.stem: My sister is ______. She always shares her food with me. Which word fits best?
hints: Sharing food shows what kind of person she is.
It is about being good to others.
