questions.explanation: A sister who always shares her food is 'kind'. Sharing shows kindness, not height, speed or noise. So 'kind' is the best word.
questions.misconception: Any adjective fits any person.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe the home, people or places

questions.stem: The library in our school is ______. Everyone must be quiet there. Which word fits best?
hints: Everyone must be quiet there.
Which word matches that?
questions.explanation: A library where everyone must be quiet is 'quiet'. 'Busy' and 'noisy' mean the opposite, and 'sweet' describes food. So 'quiet' fits best.

questions.stem: In a group of four, take turns to say one thing you like about school. Each person must get a turn. Do not interrupt.

criteria.description: Each pupil gets a turn to speak
No one interrupts while another is speaking
Each pupil says something about school
The group stays on the topic

hints: Wait for your turn.
Listen to what others say.
questions.explanation: This is a practical group task. The teacher watches for turn-taking, no interrupting, staying on topic and each pupil speaking.
questions.misconception: Interrupting is fine if you have a good point.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Engage in collaborative conversation

questions.stem: Read this dialogue: Ama: 'I went to the market.' Kofi: 'What did you buy?' Ama: 'I bought some oranges.' Who spoke last?
hints: Who spoke after Kofi asked a question?
It was the person who bought the oranges.
questions.explanation: Ama spoke last because she answered Kofi's question with 'I bought some oranges.' Kofi spoke before her, not last.
questions.misconception: The last person to start talking is the last speaker.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Engage in collaborative conversation

questions.stem: Your friend says: 'I am feeling sick today.' What is the best reply?
options: I am sorry to hear that. Do you need help?
hints: Your friend is not feeling well.
Show care and offer help.
questions.explanation: When a friend says they are sick, a caring reply like 'I am sorry to hear that. Do you need help?' shows you were listening and you care. 'That is nice!' is the wrong feeling. Talking about football changes the topic. 'Goodbye' ends the conversation.
questions.misconception: Any reply is fine, even if it does not match what was said.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Engage in collaborative conversation

questions.stem: You are talking about the weather. Which sentence does NOT stay on the topic?
options: I think it will rain tomorrow.
My mother bought a new pot.
hints: The topic is the weather.
Which sentence is about something else?
questions.explanation: 'My mother bought a new pot' is about a pot, not the weather, so it does not stay on the topic. The other sentences are all about weather.
questions.misconception: Any sentence belongs in any conversation.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Engage in collaborative conversation

questions.stem: You want to speak to your teacher, but she is talking to another teacher. What do you say?
options: Excuse me, teacher. May I speak to you, please?
Stop talking and listen to me!
hints: You are interrupting an adult conversation.
Be polite and use 'please'.
questions.explanation: 'Excuse me, teacher. May I speak to you, please?' is polite because it uses 'excuse me' and 'please' and respects the teacher's conversation. The other options are rude demands.
questions.misconception: Any way of speaking is polite.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Engage in collaborative conversation

questions.stem: In pairs, have a conversation about what you did over the weekend. Ask at least two questions and answer at least two questions. Take turns.

criteria.description: Stays on the topic of the weekend

hints: Start with 'What did you do at the weekend?'
Answer your partner, then ask another question.
questions.explanation: This is an oral pair task. The teacher listens for questions, answers, turn-taking and staying on topic.
questions.misconception: One person should do all the talking.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Engage in collaborative conversation

questions.stem: In a group of four, discuss 'What makes a good friend?' Each pupil must say one idea. Take turns. Listen to others and do not interrupt.

criteria.description: Each pupil gives one idea about a good friend
Builds on another pupil's idea (says 'I agree' or adds to it)

hints: Think of what a good friend does.
You can say 'I agree with Ama. A good friend is also...'
questions.explanation: This is a group discussion task. The teacher watches for each pupil contributing, turn-taking, staying on topic and building on others' ideas.
questions.misconception: Conversation is only about your own topic.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Engage in collaborative conversation

questions.stem: In pairs, take turns to describe your home to your partner. Each person speaks for about one minute while the other listens, then swap.

criteria.description: Speaks for the given time about the home
Listens quietly when the partner is speaking
Stays on the topic of the home

hints: Describe your home in detail.
When your partner speaks, listen and do not interrupt.
questions.explanation: This is an oral pair task. The teacher listens for a detailed description, good listening and turn-taking.
questions.misconception: Taking turns means talking at the same time.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Engage in collaborative conversation

questions.stem: In pairs, hold a conversation about 'My favourite animal'. You must: ask two questions, answer two questions, use one polite word ('please', 'thank you' or 'sorry') and take turns properly.
hints: Ask 'What is your favourite animal?' and 'Why do you like it?'
Remember to say 'thank you' or 'please'.
questions.explanation: This is an extended oral pair task. The teacher listens for questions, answers, polite words and proper turn-taking.
questions.misconception: Conversation is only about your own topic.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Engage in collaborative conversation

questions.stem: In a group of four, plan a class party. Each pupil suggests one thing (food, music, games, place). Listen to each idea, then agree on a plan together. Do not interrupt.

criteria.description: Takes turns in an orderly way
The group reaches an agreed plan

hints: Suggest your idea, then listen to others.
Try to agree on one thing together.
questions.explanation: This is a practical group task. The teacher watches for contributions, listening, turn-taking and reaching an agreement.
questions.misconception: The group leader should decide everything.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Engage in collaborative conversation

questions.stem: In a group of four, talk about 'Why we should keep our school clean.' Each pupil speaks at least once. One pupil is the timekeeper. Show good turn-taking and listening.

criteria.description: Each pupil speaks at least once on the topic
Stays on the topic of keeping the school clean

hints: Think of reasons why a clean school is good.
Wait for your turn before you speak.
questions.explanation: This is an extended group discussion task. The teacher watches for everyone contributing, turn-taking, listening and staying on topic.
questions.misconception: Interrupting is fine if you have a good point.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Engage in collaborative conversation

questions.stem: Read: 'I like rice.' What does the person like?
hints: Look for the food named after 'like'.
It is a common food.
questions.explanation: The sentence says 'I like rice', so the person likes rice. Beans, fufu and yam are not mentioned in the sentence.
questions.misconception: Any food fits the sentence.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: Read: 'I do not like snakes.' What does the person dislike?
hints: Look for the animal named after 'do not like'.
It is a long animal with no legs.
questions.explanation: The sentence says 'I do not like snakes', so the person dislikes snakes. The other animals are not mentioned in the sentence.
questions.misconception: 'Dislike' means hate strongly.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama loves her doll.' What does Ama like?
hints: Look for the toy mentioned.
It is a toy that looks like a baby.
questions.explanation: The sentence says Ama loves her doll. So Ama likes her doll. The ball, book and bag are not mentioned.
questions.misconception: Only food can be liked.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: I ______ fufu. It is my favourite food. Which word fits best?
hints: The sentence says it is the favourite food.
Favourite foods are liked.
questions.explanation: 'Favourite' means you like it best, so the correct word is 'like'. 'Hate', 'dislike' and 'do not like' mean the opposite.
questions.misconception: 'I like' and 'I don't like' mean the same.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: Kofi ______ spiders. He runs away from them. Which word fits best?
hints: Kofi runs away from spiders.
He is afraid of them.
questions.explanation: If Kofi runs away from spiders, he does not like them. 'Loves', 'likes' and 'enjoys' mean the opposite of his action.
questions.misconception: You must like everything.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: Which word means the same as 'like very much'?
hints: 'Like very much' is stronger than 'like'.
It is a warm, happy feeling.
questions.explanation: 'Love' means to like something very much. 'Hate' and 'dislike' mean the opposite, and 'do not like' is also negative.
questions.misconception: Only food can be liked.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: Ama likes mangoes. Why? Because they are ______.
hints: Mangoes are a sweet fruit.
People usually like sweet things.
questions.explanation: Mangoes are sweet, so a good reason to like them is 'because they are sweet'. Sour, bitter and hot do not describe a ripe mango.
questions.misconception: A reason can be anything.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: Kofi does not like snakes. Why? Because they are ______.
hints: Many people are afraid of snakes.
Which word describes something that makes you afraid?
questions.explanation: Snakes can be scary, so a good reason to dislike them is 'because they are scary'. Sweet and soft do not fit, and 'friendly' is the opposite of why someone would dislike them.
questions.misconception: A reason can be anything.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: Which is a good reason to like a toy car?
options: Because it is fun to play with.
hints: A toy is for playing.
Think about what you do with a toy car.
questions.explanation: A toy car is fun to play with, so 'because it is fun to play with' is a good reason to like it. Sweet, scary and sour do not describe why someone likes a toy.
questions.misconception: A reason can be anything.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama likes rice. Kofi likes beans.' Who likes beans?
hints: Look for the name next to 'beans'.
It is the boy in the sentence.
questions.explanation: The sentence says Kofi likes beans. Ama likes rice. So only Kofi likes beans.
questions.misconception: Both children like the same food.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: Read: 'Yaw does not like cats. He likes dogs.' Which animal does Yaw like?
hints: Look for the animal after 'likes'.
It is the animal he does not run away from.
questions.explanation: The sentence says Yaw likes dogs. He does not like cats. So Yaw likes dogs only.
questions.misconception: 'Dislike' means hate strongly.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: Read: 'Adjoa likes dolls. She does not like balls.' What does Adjoa dislike?
hints: Look for the toy after 'does not like'.
It is round and you can kick it.
questions.explanation: The sentence says Adjoa does not like balls, so balls are what she dislikes. She likes dolls, so dolls are not what she dislikes.
questions.misconception: 'Dislike' means hate strongly.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: Say two things you like about food and one thing you do not like about food. Use simple sentences.

criteria.description: Names one food they do not like

hints: Start with 'I like... and I like...'
Then say 'I do not like...'
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for two likes, one dislike and clear sentences.
questions.misconception: You must like everything.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: Talk about an animal you like and an animal you do not like. Say why for each.

criteria.description: Gives a reason for liking it
Names an animal they do not like
Gives a reason for not liking it

hints: Say 'I like... because...'
Then say 'I do not like... because...'
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for an animal they like with a reason and an animal they do not like with a reason.
questions.misconception: A reason can be anything.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: Describe a toy you like. Say why you like it.

criteria.description: Gives a clear reason for liking it

hints: Start with 'I like my...'
Say why: 'Because it is fun to play with.'
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for a toy name, a reason and a clear sentence.
questions.misconception: Only food can be liked.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: Talk about your favourite food and a food you do not like. Give one reason for each.

criteria.description: Gives a reason for liking it
Names a food they do not like
Gives a reason for not liking it

hints: Say 'My favourite food is... because...'
Then say 'I do not like... because...'
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for a favourite food with a reason and a disliked food with a reason.
questions.misconception: 'Dislike' means hate strongly.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: In pairs, ask your partner what food they like. Then answer when they ask you.

criteria.description: Asks the question 'What food do you like?'

hints: Start with 'What food do you like?'
Answer when your partner asks you.
questions.explanation: This is an oral pair task. The teacher listens for asking the question, answering, turn-taking and politeness.
questions.misconception: Conversation is only about your own likes.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: In pairs, ask your partner what animal they do not like. Then answer when they ask you.

criteria.description: Asks 'What animal do you not like?'

hints: Start with 'What animal do you not like?'
Answer with the animal and maybe a reason.
questions.explanation: This is an oral pair task. The teacher listens for the question, the answer, turn-taking and clear speaking.
questions.misconception: You must like everything.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: In pairs, take turns asking and answering about favourite toys. Use the question 'Do you like...?'

criteria.description: Uses 'Do you like...?' to ask about toys
Answers 'Yes, I do' or 'No, I don't'

hints: Ask 'Do you like dolls?' or 'Do you like toy cars?'
Answer 'Yes, I do' or 'No, I don't'.
questions.explanation: This is an oral pair task. The teacher listens for the question form, the answers and turn-taking.
questions.misconception: Only food can be liked.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: In pairs, have a conversation about likes and dislikes. Ask two questions and answer two questions.

criteria.description: Asks two clear questions about likes/dislikes

hints: Ask about food, animals and toys.
Answer each question your partner asks.
questions.explanation: This is an oral pair task. The teacher listens for two questions, two answers, turn-taking and polite speaking.
questions.misconception: 'Dislike' means hate strongly.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Talk about likes and dislikes: food, animals, toys, etc.

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama has a small black cat. The cat likes milk. Ama gives the cat milk every morning.' Who is in the story?
hints: Listen for the names in the story.
One is a girl and one is an animal.
questions.explanation: The story is about Ama and her black cat. Kofi, the dog, the farmer, the cow, the teacher and the pupil are not in this story.
questions.misconception: Any name fits the story.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kofi went to the market. He bought two oranges. He ate one orange on the way home.' What did Kofi buy?
hints: Listen for the name of the fruit.
It is round and orange in colour.
questions.explanation: The story says Kofi bought two oranges. Mangoes, bananas and apples are not mentioned in the story.
questions.misconception: Any fruit fits the story.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: The title of the story is 'The Thirsty Crow'. The picture shows a crow standing near a pot of water. What do you think the story is about?
options: A crow sleeping under a tree
hints: The title says 'thirsty'.
The picture shows a pot of water.
questions.explanation: A thirsty crow near a pot of water suggests the story is about a crow looking for water. Eating rice, flying to school or sleeping do not match the title or the picture.
questions.misconception: Prediction = guessing anything.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama found a small bird. The bird had a hurt wing. Ama put the bird in a box. She gave it food. The bird got well and flew away.' Now retell the story using the three pictures your teacher shows you.

criteria.description: Names the characters (Ama and the bird)
Says what happened in the correct order
Says how the story ended (the bird flew away)

hints: Look at the pictures in order.
Start with who is in the story.
questions.explanation: This is an oral retelling task. The teacher listens for characters, correct order, the ending and clear speech.
questions.misconception: Retelling means repeating every exact word.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kofi woke up late. He could not find his uniform. His mother helped him look. The uniform was under the bed. Kofi dressed quickly and ran to school.' Now retell the story in your own words.

criteria.description: Tells the beginning of the story
Tells the middle of the story
Tells the end of the story

hints: Think about how Kofi's day started.
Then say what happened next.
questions.explanation: This is an oral retelling task. The teacher listens for beginning, middle, end and clear speech.
questions.misconception: A retell can stop in the middle.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'The class went to the zoo. They saw a big lion. The lion was sleeping under a tree. The pupils were quiet so they would not wake the lion.' What did the class see?
hints: Listen for the animal named in the story.
It was sleeping under a tree.
questions.explanation: The story says the class saw a big lion. No elephant, monkey or snake is mentioned in the story.
questions.misconception: Any animal fits the story.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama went to the river to fetch water. The pot was heavy. She rested under a tree. A kind woman helped her carry the pot. Ama thanked her.' What is the most important event in the story?
options: Ama fetched water from the river
The kind woman helped Ama carry the pot
hints: What solved Ama's problem?
The pot was too heavy for her.
questions.explanation: Ama's problem was the heavy pot. The key event is when the kind woman helps her carry it. Resting and thanking are smaller parts of the story.
questions.misconception: A small detail is the key event.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kwame woke up early. He washed his face. He ate his food. He took his bag. He went to school.' Now retell the story in the correct order, using the pictures your teacher shows you.

criteria.description: Retells the events in the correct order
Includes all the key actions (woke, washed, ate, took bag, went to school)
Uses own words (not just repeating exactly)

hints: Follow the pictures from left to right.
What did Kwame do first?
questions.explanation: This is an oral retelling task. The teacher listens for correct order, key actions, own words and clear speech.
questions.misconception: Order does not matter in a retell.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama and Kofi went to the market. Ama bought a mango. Kofi bought a banana. They shared the fruit and ate it on the way home.' Now work with a partner to act out the main events of the story.

criteria.description: Stays in role as Ama or Kofi
Acts the main events in order (went to market, bought fruit, shared and ate)
Uses words and actions that match the story
Works with the partner without grabbing parts

hints: One of you is Ama, one is Kofi.
Act out buying fruit and sharing it.
questions.explanation: This is a practical role-play task. The teacher watches for staying in role, correct order, matching actions and cooperation.
questions.misconception: Role-play is just talking.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Yaw went to the farm with his father. They planted maize. Yaw carried a small hoe. His father carried a big hoe.' What did Yaw and his father plant?
hints: Listen for the crop name.
It is a common grain in Ghana.
questions.explanation: The story says Yaw and his father planted maize. Maize is also called corn. So either 'maize' or 'corn' is correct.
questions.misconception: Any crop fits the story.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen to the beginning of a story: 'The sun was very hot. Ama was walking home from school. She felt very thirsty.' What do you think Ama will do next?
options: Ama will look for water to drink
hints: Ama is thirsty.
What do thirsty people need?
questions.explanation: Ama is thirsty, so she will look for water to drink. Sleeping, playing football or eating rice do not solve thirst.
questions.misconception: Prediction = guessing anything.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kofi lost his pencil. He looked under the table. He looked in his bag. Ama said, "Here is your pencil. It fell near the door." Kofi was happy.' What is the key event in the story?
hints: What solved Kofi's problem?
He could not find his pencil.
questions.explanation: Kofi's problem was losing his pencil. The key event is when Ama finds it and tells him where it was. Looking under the table and in his bag did not solve the problem.
questions.misconception: A small detail is the key event.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Maame Adwoa sold oranges at the market. Every day, a boy named Yaw bought two oranges. One day, Yaw did not come. Maame Adwoa asked about him. She learned that Yaw was sick. She took oranges to Yaw's house. Yaw's mother thanked her.' Why did Maame Adwoa take oranges to Yaw's house?
options: Because Yaw was at the market
hints: Listen for the reason she took the oranges.
It is about Yaw's health.
questions.explanation: The story says Maame Adwoa learned that Yaw was sick, so she took oranges to him. Hunger, school and the market are not the reasons given in the story.
questions.misconception: Any answer sounds right.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'The rain started. Ama ran home. She was wet. She changed her clothes. Her mother made her warm tea.' Which is the KEY event that must be in a retell?
options: Ama ran home in the rain and got wet
hints: What is the main thing that happened to Ama?
It caused her to change her clothes.
questions.explanation: The key event is that Ama ran home in the rain and got wet, which led to her changing clothes and drinking tea. The colour of the clothes and the size of the house are not in the story.
questions.misconception: A small detail is the key event.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kofi and Ama went to the river. Kofi slipped and fell into the water. Ama shouted for help. A fisherman heard her. He pulled Kofi out. The fisherman said, "Take care near the water." The two children went home.' Now retell the story with a clear beginning, middle and end.

criteria.description: Names the beginning (Kofi and Ama went to the river)
Names the middle (Kofi fell in and Ama shouted for help)
Names the end (the fisherman pulled Kofi out and they went home)
Speaks clearly and uses complete sentences

hints: Who went to the river first?
What happened in the middle?
How did the story end?
questions.explanation: This is an oral retelling task. The teacher listens for beginning, middle, end and clear speech.
questions.misconception: A retell can skip the end.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama found a small bird. The bird had a hurt wing. Ama put the bird in a box. She gave it food and water. The bird got well and flew away.' Now work in a group of three to act out the story. One pupil is the narrator, one is Ama, and one is the bird.

criteria.description: Each pupil stays in their role
Acts the main events in order (finds bird, cares for it, bird flies away)
Uses words and actions that match the story
The group works together without interrupting

hints: The narrator tells the story while the others act.
The bird should look hurt, then fly away at the end.
questions.explanation: This is a group role-play task. The teacher watches for staying in role, correct order, matching actions and cooperation.
questions.misconception: Role-play is just talking.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen to the beginning of a story: 'Kofi was walking to school. He saw a small bag on the ground. He picked it up. There was money inside.' What do you think Kofi will do next?
options: Kofi will look for the owner of the bag
Kofi will throw the bag away
hints: What is the right thing to do with something you find?
The bag has an owner.
questions.explanation: The right thing to do is to look for the owner of the bag. Keeping the money is wrong, throwing it away is wasteful, and going home does not solve the problem.
questions.misconception: Prediction = guessing anything.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama was carrying a heavy pot of water. She could not carry it alone. She sat down under a tree. A kind woman came. The woman helped Ama carry the pot. Ama thanked her.' Now work with a partner to act out the problem and the solution.

criteria.description: Shows the problem clearly (Ama cannot carry the pot)
Shows the solution clearly (the kind woman helps)
Works with the partner to show the sequence

hints: One of you is Ama and one is the kind woman.
First show Ama struggling, then show the help.
questions.explanation: This is a partner role-play task. The teacher watches for a clear problem, a clear solution, staying in role and cooperation.
questions.misconception: The problem and solution can be shown in any order.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'A greedy dog found a piece of meat. He was crossing a river. He saw another dog in the water with a bigger piece of meat. He opened his mouth to grab it. His own meat fell into the water. The greedy dog lost his meat.' Now retell the story in your own words. At the end, say what lesson the story teaches.

criteria.description: Retells the story in the correct order
Includes the key event (the dog lost his meat)
States a clear lesson (do not be greedy)

hints: Think about what the dog saw in the water.
What happened when he opened his mouth?
questions.explanation: This is an extended oral retelling task. The teacher listens for correct order, the key event, a moral lesson and clear speech.
questions.misconception: A retell can skip the lesson.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'The lion was big and proud. He laughed at the small ant. The ant said, "I am small but I can help you." One day the lion was caught in a net. He roared for help. The ant came with many ants. They cut the net with their strong jaws. The lion was free. The lion thanked the ant.' Now in a group of four, act out the story. One pupil is the narrator; the others are the lion, the ant and the other ants. Show the problem, the solution and the ending.

criteria.description: Each pupil stays in role throughout
Shows the problem clearly (lion caught in the net)
Shows the solution clearly (ants cut the net)
The group works together in the correct order

hints: The lion starts big and proud, then gets stuck.
The ants work together to free him.
questions.explanation: This is a group role-play task. The teacher watches for staying in role, a clear problem, a clear solution and cooperation.
questions.misconception: Role-play is just talking.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and reproduce narrative texts

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama woke up early. She washed her face. She went to school.' What happened at the BEGINNING of the story?
hints: What is the very first thing Ama did?
It is the first sentence.
questions.explanation: The story begins with 'Ama woke up early.' Washing and going to school happen after she wakes up. So the beginning is 'Ama woke up early.'
questions.misconception: The last action is the beginning.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kofi found a mango. He washed it. He ate it.' What happened at the END of the story?
hints: What is the last thing Kofi did?
It comes after washing.
questions.explanation: The last thing Kofi does in the story is eat the mango. Finding and washing come first. Sleeping is not in the story.
questions.misconception: The first thing is the ending.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama woke up. She ate her food. She went to school.' What happened in the MIDDLE of the story?
hints: What comes between waking up and going to school?
It is something she ate.
questions.explanation: The order is: woke up, ate her food, went to school. So the middle event is 'She ate her food.' Waking up is the start and going to school is the end.
questions.misconception: The middle is the start.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'The sun was hot. Ama took her umbrella. She walked to the market. She bought rice.' What happened at the BEGINNING of the story?
hints: What is the first sentence of the story?
It is about the weather.
questions.explanation: The first sentence says 'The sun was hot.' The other events happen after. So the beginning is 'The sun was hot.'
questions.misconception: The most important event comes first.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kwame washed his hands. He sat at the table. He ate his lunch.' What happened at the END of the story?
hints: What is the last action in the story?
It is something to do with food.
questions.explanation: The last action in the story is Kwame eating his lunch. Washing his hands and sitting at the table happen before.
questions.misconception: The first action is the ending.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama woke up. She washed her face. She went to school.' Which order is correct?
options: Washed her face → Woke up → Went to school
Went to school → Woke up → Washed her face
Ama woke up → Washed her face → Went to school
Ama woke up → Went to school → Washed her face
hints: What is the first thing Ama did?
Washing comes before going to school.
questions.explanation: The story order is: she woke up, then washed her face, then went to school. Only option 3 follows that order.
questions.misconception: Order does not matter.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kofi went to the market. He bought a mango. He ate the mango. He went home.' Which order is correct?
options: Went to market → Ate the mango → Bought the mango → Went home
Went to market → Bought the mango → Ate the mango → Went home
Went home → Went to market → Bought the mango → Ate the mango
Bought the mango → Went to market → Ate the mango → Went home
hints: What did Kofi do first?
He must buy the mango before he eats it.
questions.explanation: Kofi goes to the market first, then buys a mango, then eats it, then goes home. He cannot eat before buying. Only option 2 follows this order.
questions.misconception: Order does not matter.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'The class went to the zoo. They saw a big lion. Ama was afraid. Kofi held her hand. The class went home.' What happened in the MIDDLE of the story?
options: The class went to the zoo
Ama was afraid and Kofi held her hand
hints: What happened after they saw the lion but before they went home?
Ama was scared.
questions.explanation: The middle of the story is when Ama was afraid and Kofi held her hand. Going to the zoo is the beginning, going home is the end, and no elephant is mentioned.
questions.misconception: The middle is the beginning.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama found a small bird. The bird had a hurt wing. Ama put the bird in a box. She gave it food and water. The bird got well and flew away.' How did the story BEGIN?
options: Ama put the bird in a box
hints: What is the very first thing that happened?
Ama found something.
questions.explanation: The story begins with 'Ama found a small bird.' Putting it in a box and giving it food come later. The bird flying away is the end.
questions.misconception: The most exciting event comes first.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kofi found a coin on the road. He picked it up. He put it in his pocket. He bought sweets with it. He shared the sweets with his sister.' How did the story END?
options: Kofi shared sweets with his sister
Kofi put the coin in his pocket
hints: What is the last thing that happened?
It involves his sister.
questions.explanation: The last action in the story is Kofi sharing the sweets with his sister. Finding the coin, picking it up and putting it in the pocket happen before.
questions.misconception: The start is the ending.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kofi washed his hands. He sat at the table. He ate his food.' What happened in the MIDDLE of the story?
hints: What comes between washing hands and eating food?
It involves a table.
questions.explanation: The order is: washed his hands, sat at the table, ate his food. The middle event is 'He sat at the table.'
questions.misconception: The middle is the first event.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama woke up early. She washed her face. She ate her food. She went to school.' Which event was NOT in the story?
hints: Which event is not in the story?
Think about where Ama went after eating.
questions.explanation: The story says Ama woke up, washed her face, ate her food and went to school. Playing football is not in the story, so it is the odd one out.
questions.misconception: Any event from another story can fit.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads a short story. Then talk about what happened at the beginning, in the middle and at the end.

criteria.description: Puts the three events in the correct order

hints: What happened first?
What happened next?
How did it end?
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for beginning, middle and end events in the correct order.
questions.misconception: Order does not matter.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama went to the market. She bought oranges. She walked home. She gave the oranges to her mother.' Talk about the beginning, middle and end of this story.

criteria.description: Names the beginning (Ama went to the market)
Names the end (she gave the oranges to her mother)

hints: Where did Ama go first?
What did she buy?
What did she do with the oranges?
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for beginning, middle and end in the correct order.
questions.misconception: The first sentence is always the beginning.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'It was a hot afternoon. Ama was walking home from school. She saw an old man carrying a heavy bag. Ama helped the old man. The old man gave her a sweet. Ama walked home happily.' How did the story BEGIN?
options: The old man gave her a sweet
hints: Which sentence comes first in the story?
It describes the weather.
questions.explanation: The very first sentence is 'It was a hot afternoon.' Everything else comes after. So the beginning is 'It was a hot afternoon.'
questions.misconception: The most interesting part is the beginning.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'The rain started. Ama ran home. She was wet. She changed her clothes.' Which order is correct?
options: The rain started → She changed her clothes → She was wet → Ama ran home
The rain started → Ama ran home → She was wet → She changed her clothes
Ama ran home → The rain started → She was wet → She changed her clothes
She changed her clothes → The rain started → Ama ran home → She was wet
hints: The rain comes first.
She can only change her clothes after she is wet.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: rain starts, Ama runs home, she is wet, she changes her clothes. Only option 2 follows this order.
questions.misconception: Order does not matter.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'The class went to the zoo. They saw a big lion. Ama was afraid. Kofi held her hand. The class went home.' What happened in the MIDDLE of the story?
options: The class went to the zoo
Ama was afraid and Kofi held her hand
hints: What happened after they saw the lion but before they went home?
Ama was scared.
questions.explanation: The middle of the story is when Ama was afraid and Kofi held her hand. Going to the zoo is the beginning, going home is the end, and no elephant is mentioned.
questions.misconception: The middle is the beginning.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kofi found a mango. He washed it. He ate it. He threw the seed away.' Which event was NOT in the story?
hints: What did Kofi do with the mango?
Did he share it with anyone or sell it?
questions.explanation: The story says Kofi found, washed and ate the mango, then threw the seed away. There is no mention of selling the mango.
questions.misconception: Any event from another story can fit.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kofi and Ama went to the river. Kofi slipped and fell into the water. Ama shouted for help. A fisherman heard her. He pulled Kofi out. The fisherman said, "Take care near the water." The two children went home.' Tell the beginning, middle and end of this story in your own words.

criteria.description: Tells the beginning (Kofi and Ama went to the river)
Tells the middle (Kofi fell in and Ama shouted for help)
Tells the end (the fisherman pulled Kofi out and they went home)
Uses own words and speaks clearly

hints: Where did they go first?
What went wrong in the middle?
How did it end?
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for beginning, middle and end in order, using own words.
questions.misconception: Beginning/middle/end are just labels.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'A greedy dog found a piece of meat. He was crossing a river. He saw another dog in the water with a bigger piece of meat. He opened his mouth to grab it. His own meat fell into the water. The greedy dog lost his meat.' Tell the beginning, middle and end of the story, and say what lesson it teaches.

criteria.description: Tells the beginning (the dog found meat and crossed the river)
Tells the middle (the dog saw another dog with bigger meat)
Tells the end (the dog lost his meat)
States a lesson (do not be greedy)

hints: What did the dog find first?
What did he see in the water?
What happened to his own meat?
questions.explanation: This is an extended oral task. The teacher listens for beginning, middle, end and a clear lesson.
questions.misconception: A story has no lesson.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama found a small bird with a hurt wing. She put it in a box. She gave it food and water. The bird got well and flew away.' Which event does NOT belong in this story?
options: Ama put the bird in a box
The bird got well and flew away
Ama sold the bird at the market
hints: What did Ama do with the bird?
Did she sell it?
questions.explanation: The story says Ama found the bird, put it in a box, gave it food and water, and the bird flew away. There is no mention of selling the bird.
questions.misconception: Any event from another story can fit.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in a narrative text

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama has a small cat. The cat is black. Ama feeds the cat every day.' Who is in the story?
hints: Listen for the names in the story.
One is a girl and one is an animal.
questions.explanation: The story names Ama and her cat. Kofi, the dog, the farmer, the cow, the teacher and the pupil are not in the story. So the characters are Ama and her cat.
questions.misconception: Any name fits the story.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Adjoa is a kind girl. She helps her mother in the house. She helps her father in the garden. Everybody loves Adjoa.' Who is the main character?
hints: Who is the story mostly about?
Whose name is repeated most?
questions.explanation: The story is mostly about Adjoa. Her name appears most often and the story tells what she does. The mother, father and everybody are in the story but are not the main character.
questions.misconception: The first person mentioned is the main character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kwame has a goat. Kwame ties the goat to a tree. The goat eats grass.' What does Kwame do?
options: He ties the goat to a tree
hints: Find what Kwame does in the story.
It is about the goat and a tree.
questions.explanation: The story says Kwame ties the goat to a tree. The goat eats grass, not Kwame. Kwame does not sleep or run away.
questions.misconception: Role = name only.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kofi went to the market with his mother. He bought a mango. The seller smiled at him.' Who is a minor character?
hints: Who appears for just a small moment?
The story is mostly about Kofi.
questions.explanation: The seller appears only for a moment (she smiles) and the story is not about her. So she is a minor character. The market and mango are not characters.
questions.misconception: Any named person is the main character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama is a tall girl with short hair. She is kind and helpful.' Now describe Ama in one or two simple sentences.

criteria.description: Says at least one thing about Ama's appearance (tall, short hair)
Says at least one thing about her character (kind, helpful)

hints: What does Ama look like?
What kind of person is she?
questions.explanation: This is an oral description task. The teacher listens for a description that includes appearance and character in complete sentences.
questions.misconception: Description = name only.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'The sun was hot. Kofi and Ama walked to school. A dog followed them. The dog was friendly.' Who are the characters in the story?
hints: Look for the names and the animal.
Three characters are mentioned.
questions.explanation: The characters are Kofi, Ama and the dog. The sun and the school are not characters. So the correct answer is Kofi, Ama and the dog.
questions.misconception: Only the people are characters.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Abena has a small brother. His name is Kojo. Kojo cries a lot. Abena sings to him. Kojo stops crying and sleeps.' What does Abena do?
hints: Find what Abena does to help.
It stops Kojo from crying.
questions.explanation: Abena sings to Kojo. Kojo cries and sleeps, not Abena. She does not eat food in the story. So her role is to sing to her brother.
questions.misconception: Role = the other character's action.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'A big lion lived in the forest. One day the lion could not find food. He walked and walked. He saw a small ant. The ant was too small to eat. The lion sat down and cried.' Who is the main character?
hints: Who is the story mostly about?
Whose name is said most?
questions.explanation: The story is mostly about the lion — it tells what the lion did and how he felt. The ant appears only at the end. The forest is a setting, not a character.
questions.misconception: The last character mentioned is the main character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Musa went to the farm. He planted maize. His sister Fatima came to help. A bird sang in a tree nearby.' Who is a minor character?
hints: Which character appears only for a small moment?
The story is mostly about Musa.
questions.explanation: The bird appears only once, singing in a tree. Fatima comes to help Musa and is part of the action, but the bird is a minor character with a small part. Maize is not a character.
questions.misconception: Anyone mentioned is the main character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ekua has a pet rabbit. The rabbit is white. Ekua feeds the rabbit with carrots.' Name the characters in the story.
hints: Look for names and animals.
One is a girl and one is a small animal.
questions.explanation: The characters are Ekua and her rabbit. Both are named or described in the story. Carrots are not a character.
questions.misconception: Only the first character counts.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Yaw has a dog. The dog is brown. Yaw plays with the dog in the evening. The dog runs after a ball.' What does the dog do?
hints: Find what the dog does in the story.
It plays with Yaw.
questions.explanation: The dog runs after a ball. The story does not say the dog eats rice, sleeps all day or sings. So the correct answer is 'it runs after a ball.'
questions.misconception: Any animal action fits.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama and her mother went to the market. Ama bought a mango. Her mother bought rice.' With your partner, talk about: (1) who is in the story, (2) what each person bought.

criteria.description: Takes turns with the partner and listens

hints: Who went to the market?
What did each person buy?
questions.explanation: This is an oral discussion task. The teacher listens for both characters, what each bought, and turn-taking.
questions.misconception: Discussion = just naming characters.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kofi found a small bird with a hurt wing. He put the bird in a box and gave it food. The bird got well and flew away. Kofi was happy.' With your partner, talk about: (1) who is in the story, (2) what Kofi did, (3) how Kofi felt at the end.

criteria.description: Says what Kofi did (put bird in box, gave food)

hints: Who is in the story?
What did Kofi do for the bird?
How did Kofi feel when the bird flew away?
questions.explanation: This is an oral discussion task. The teacher listens for characters, actions and feelings, plus turn-taking.
questions.misconception: A character's feelings are not part of who they are.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kojo lost his pencil. He looked under the table. He looked in his bag. Ama said, "Here is your pencil. It fell near the door." Kojo was happy.' What is Ama's role in the story?
options: She helps Kojo find his pencil
hints: What does Ama say to Kojo?
Her words give Kojo the answer.
questions.explanation: Ama tells Kojo where his pencil is, so she helps him find it. Kojo is the one who loses the pencil and looks under the table. The story does not say Ama is a teacher.
questions.misconception: Role = name only.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'There was a big fire in the forest. All the animals ran away. The rabbit did not run. The rabbit ran to the river. It carried water in a small leaf. It tried to put out the fire. The elephant saw the rabbit and helped.' Who is the main character?
hints: Who does most of the actions in the story?
The elephant only appears at the end.
questions.explanation: The rabbit is in almost every sentence — it does not run, it goes to the river, it carries water, it tries to put out the fire. The elephant appears only at the end. So the rabbit is the main character.
questions.misconception: The biggest animal is the main character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Mr Mensah is a teacher. He teaches English in a school. His class has twenty pupils. One pupil is Adjoa. She loves reading. A visitor came to watch the class. Mr Mensah greeted the visitor.' Who is a minor character?
hints: Which person appears only once and does not do much?
The story is about Mr Mensah and his class.
questions.explanation: The visitor comes to watch and is greeted — they appear once at the end and have only one small action. Mr Mensah and Adjoa are more important to the story. The class is not a character.
questions.misconception: Anyone mentioned is a main character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Kofi is a tall boy with short hair. He is kind. He helped his friend find his bag.' Describe Kofi in one or two simple sentences.

criteria.description: Says one thing about Kofi's appearance (tall, short hair)
Says one thing about his character (kind, helpful)

hints: What does Kofi look like?
What kind of person is he?
questions.explanation: This is an oral description task. The teacher listens for appearance, character and complete sentences.
questions.misconception: Description = name only.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Ama and her mother went to the market. Ama bought a mango. Her mother bought rice. On the way home, it started to rain. Ama was wet. Her mother gave her an umbrella. Ama was happy.' With your partner, discuss: (1) who is in the story, (2) what happened at the market, (3) what happened on the way home, (4) how Ama felt at the end.

criteria.description: Says what happened at the market (Ama bought mango, mother bought rice)
Says what happened on the way home (rain started, mother gave umbrella)

hints: Who went to the market?
What did they buy?
What happened on the way home?
How did Ama feel?
questions.explanation: This is an extended oral discussion task. The teacher listens for characters, events and feelings, plus clear discussion.
questions.misconception: Discussion = just naming characters.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'The lion was big and proud. He had a loud roar. He laughed at the small ant. The ant was brave and clever. The ant helped the lion when he was caught in a net.' Describe the lion in two simple sentences.

criteria.description: Says one thing about the lion's appearance or behaviour (big, proud, loud roar)
Says one thing about the lion's character (proud, unkind)

hints: What does the lion look like?
What kind of character is the lion?
questions.explanation: This is an extended oral description task. The teacher listens for two sentences that describe the lion's appearance and character.
questions.misconception: Description = name only.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'Maame Adwoa sold oranges at the market. Every day, Yaw bought two oranges. One day Yaw did not come. Maame Adwoa asked about him. She learned Yaw was sick. She took oranges to Yaw's house. Yaw's mother thanked her.' With your partner, discuss: (1) who is in the story, (2) what Maame Adwoa did when Yaw did not come, (3) how you think Yaw felt when he saw Maame Adwoa.

criteria.description: Names the characters (Maame Adwoa, Yaw, Yaw's mother)
Says what Maame Adwoa did (asked about Yaw, took oranges to his house)
Gives an opinion on how Yaw felt
Takes turns and listens to the partner

hints: Who is in the story?
What did Maame Adwoa do for Yaw?
How would you feel if someone brought you oranges when you were sick?
questions.explanation: This is an extended oral discussion task. The teacher listens for characters, actions, opinions about feelings and good discussion skills.
questions.misconception: Discussion = just naming characters.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Recognise and discuss characters in a story

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'It is round. It is orange. You can eat it. It is sweet.' Which picture matches?
hints: The fruit is orange in colour.
It is round and sweet.
questions.explanation: The description says round, orange and sweet. An orange fits this. A banana is long and yellow, a mango is usually yellow or green, and a tomato is red.
questions.misconception: Description = naming the object only.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and produce descriptions of pictures and objects (e.g. vehicles, animals)

questions.stem: Look at the picture of a ball. Which sentence best describes the ball?
options: The ball is round and red.
The ball is long and green.
The ball is square and blue.
The ball is tall and yellow.
hints: What shape is a ball?
What colour is the ball in the picture?
questions.explanation: A ball is round, not long, square or tall. In the picture, the ball is red. So the best description is 'The ball is round and red.'
questions.misconception: Any adjective fits any object.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and produce descriptions of pictures and objects (e.g. vehicles, animals)

questions.stem: Look at the picture of a dog. What does the dog look like?
options: It has four legs and a tail.
It has two legs and wings.
hints: How many legs does a dog have?
What does a dog wag?
questions.explanation: A dog has four legs and a tail. Two legs and wings describe a bird. No legs describes a snake. Six legs describe an insect like an ant.
questions.misconception: All animals are 'dogs'.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and produce descriptions of pictures and objects (e.g. vehicles, animals)

questions.stem: Look at the picture of a car. What is the car used for?
hints: Where does a car travel?
What does a car carry?
questions.explanation: A car is used for carrying people on the road. It does not fly, sail or cook food. Those are other vehicles or objects.
questions.misconception: All vehicles are 'cars'.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and produce descriptions of pictures and objects (e.g. vehicles, animals)

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads: 'It has four legs. It has a tail. It says "meow".' Which animal is this?
hints: The animal says 'meow'.
It has four legs and a tail.
questions.explanation: 'Meow' is the sound a cat makes. A dog barks, a goat bleats and a cow moos. So the correct animal is a cat.
questions.misconception: All animals are 'dogs'.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Listen to and produce descriptions of pictures and objects (e.g. vehicles, animals)

questions.stem: Look at the picture of a table in a classroom. Which sentence best describes the table?
options: The table is long and brown.
The table is short and green.
The table is round and blue.
The table is tiny and white.

questions.stem: Your friend asks: 'Could you please lend me your ruler? I will give it back after class.' Which is the most polite response?
options: Yes, of course. Here you are.
hints: The request is polite.
Respond with a polite yes.
questions.explanation: 'Yes, of course. Here you are' is the most polite response. It agrees to the request in a kind way. The other options are rude or unhelpful.
questions.misconception: Any answer is a polite response.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.sub_strand: 9: Giving and Responding to Commands/Instructions and Making Requests
questions.objective: Make and respond to polite requests using the word "Please"

questions.stem: In pairs, act out a scene where one pupil wants to borrow a book from the other. The pupil must make a polite request using 'please'. The other pupil must respond politely, either by accepting or politely declining with a reason. Then swap.

criteria.description: Responds politely (accepts or declines with a reason)
Takes turns and stays on the scene

hints: Make a polite request first.
If you cannot lend the book, say 'I'm sorry, I can't. I need it now.'
questions.explanation: This is an extended oral pair task. The teacher listens for polite requests, polite responses (accept or decline with reason), kind tone and turn-taking.
questions.misconception: 'No' is always rude.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.sub_strand: 9: Giving and Responding to Commands/Instructions and Making Requests
questions.objective: Make and respond to polite requests using the word "Please"

questions.stem: In a group of three, take turns making and responding to polite requests. Each pupil must make one request, respond to one request, and politely decline one request with a reason. Use 'please' and 'thank you'.

criteria.description: Politely declines one request with a reason

hints: Plan who will make which request.
Remember to say 'please' when asking and 'thank you' when receiving.
questions.explanation: This is an extended group task. The teacher listens for polite requests, polite responses, polite refusals with reasons and good turn-taking.
questions.misconception: 'No' is always rude.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.sub_strand: 9: Giving and Responding to Commands/Instructions and Making Requests
questions.objective: Make and respond to polite requests using the word "Please"

questions.stem: Ama is presenting 'My Family' to her classmates in class. Who is her audience?
hints: Who is she speaking to?
The people listening are the audience.
questions.explanation: Ama is presenting to her classmates, so they are her audience. Her family, the head teacher and the whole school are not the people listening in this case.
questions.misconception: Audience is always the teacher.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: Kofi stands up to tell the class about his new pet dog. What is the purpose of his presentation?
hints: He is telling them about something new.
The purpose is to give information.
questions.explanation: Kofi is telling the class about his new pet dog, so the purpose is to inform. Entertaining, thanking or asking for money are different purposes.
questions.misconception: Purpose is always 'to get marks'.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: Which audience is best for a presentation titled 'My Friend'?
hints: A presentation about a friend is personal and friendly.
Who would enjoy hearing about a friend?
questions.explanation: A presentation titled 'My Friend' is personal and friendly, so classmates at a birthday party are the best audience. The head teacher, cook or driver would not be the best audience for this topic.
questions.misconception: Any topic fits any audience.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: You are presenting 'My Family' to your classmates. Which opening line is best?
options: Good morning, everyone. Today I will talk about my family.
Good morning, head teacher. My family is big.
Hello, cook. I have a family.
Goodbye, everyone. My family is here.
hints: The audience is your classmates.
Start by greeting them and saying your topic.
questions.explanation: 'Good morning, everyone. Today I will talk about my family' is the best opening because it greets the audience (classmates) and states the topic. The other openings address the wrong people or are not appropriate.
questions.misconception: Speaking to parents is the same as speaking to classmates.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: Ama is presenting 'Our School Rules' to her classmates. She starts by saying, 'Good morning, my dear family. Today I will talk about my pet.' What is wrong with her presentation?
options: She is speaking to the wrong audience and the wrong topic.
She is not wearing a uniform.
hints: Who is she actually speaking to? Who should she speak to?
What is her topic?
questions.explanation: Ama's presentation is wrong because she is addressing her family instead of her classmates, and she says she will talk about her pet instead of school rules. The audience and purpose do not match.
questions.misconception: Introduction and purpose are the same thing.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: Kwame is presenting 'Why We Should Keep Our School Clean' to the whole school at assembly. Who is his audience?
hints: Where is he presenting?
Who is listening at assembly?
questions.explanation: Kwame is presenting at assembly to the whole school, so his audience is the whole school. Only his teacher or only his classmates would be a smaller audience, and people at the market are not present.
questions.misconception: Audience is always the teacher.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: Adjoa is presenting 'The Story of the Greedy Dog' to her class. What is the purpose of her presentation?
hints: She is telling a story.
Stories are meant to be enjoyable.
questions.explanation: Adjoa is telling a story, so the purpose is to entertain. Informing is giving facts, thanking is showing gratitude, and instructing is teaching how to do something.
questions.misconception: Purpose is always 'to get marks'.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: Which audience is best for a presentation titled 'How to Keep Our School Clean'?
hints: The topic is about the school.
Who needs to hear about keeping the school clean?
questions.explanation: The whole school at assembly is the best audience for 'How to Keep Our School Clean' because the topic is about the school. The people at the market, babies and drivers are not the right audience.
questions.misconception: Any topic fits any audience.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: You are presenting 'Thank You, Teachers' at a school event for teachers. Which opening line is best?
options: Good morning, teachers. Today I want to say thank you for all you do.
Good morning, fellow pupils. Let us talk about football.
Good morning, cook. The food is nice.
Good morning, driver. Thank you for driving.
hints: The audience is teachers.
The purpose is to thank them.
questions.explanation: 'Good morning, teachers. Today I want to say thank you for all you do' is the best opening because it addresses the correct audience (teachers) and states the purpose (thanking them). The others address different people or different topics.
questions.misconception: Speaking to parents is the same as speaking to classmates.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: Kofi is presenting 'My Favourite Food' to his classmates. He says, 'Good morning, head teacher. Today I will talk about the school rules.' What is wrong?
options: He is addressing the head teacher instead of his classmates, and talking about the wrong topic.
hints: Who is the audience supposed to be?
What is the topic supposed to be?
questions.explanation: Kofi's presentation is wrong because he addresses the head teacher instead of his classmates, and he says he will talk about school rules instead of his favourite food. The audience and purpose are both incorrect.
questions.misconception: Introduction and purpose are the same thing.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: You are going to present 'My School' to your classmates. Say who your audience is and what your purpose is.
hints: Who will listen to you?
What do you want them to learn?
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for correct audience (classmates) and purpose (to inform or describe).
questions.misconception: Audience is always the teacher.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: You are going to present 'Thank You, Teachers' at a school assembly. Say who your audience is and what your purpose is.
hints: Who are you thanking?
What is the purpose of your talk?
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for correct audience (teachers/whole school) and purpose (to thank).
questions.misconception: Purpose is always 'to get marks'.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation
