criteria.description: Explains why the audience and purpose fit (classmates enjoy stories)

hints: Who enjoys stories?
Why is it good to tell stories to your classmates?
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for correct audience, purpose, a simple reason, and clear speech.
questions.misconception: Any topic fits any audience.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: You are presenting 'How to Keep Our School Clean' to the whole school at assembly. Say who your audience is, what your purpose is, and give one reason why this presentation suits this audience.

criteria.description: Gives a reason why it suits the audience (everyone uses the school)

hints: Who needs to keep the school clean?
Why is assembly a good time to talk about this?
questions.explanation: This is an extended oral task. The teacher listens for correct audience, purpose, a clear reason and confident speech.
questions.misconception: Audience is always the teacher.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: Ama is presenting 'My Pet' to her classmates. Who is her audience?
hints: Who is she speaking to?
They are in the same class as her.
questions.explanation: Ama's audience is her classmates. They are the ones listening to her presentation.
questions.misconception: Audience is always the teacher.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: Kofi is presenting 'Why We Should Not Waste Water' to his class. What is the purpose of his presentation?
hints: He is giving reasons to do something.
The purpose is to give information or persuade.
questions.explanation: The purpose is to inform or persuade the class about not wasting water. Any answer that shows he is giving information or convincing them is correct.
questions.misconception: Purpose is always 'to get marks'.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: You are presenting 'My Favourite Animal' to your classmates. Which opening line is best?
options: Good morning, classmates. Today I will talk about my favourite animal.
Good morning, head teacher. My animal is a dog.
Good morning, cook. I have a cat.
hints: The audience is your classmates.
Start with a greeting and state your topic.
questions.explanation: 'Good morning, classmates. Today I will talk about my favourite animal' is the best opening because it greets the correct audience and states the topic. The others address the wrong people or are not proper openings.
questions.misconception: Speaking to parents is the same as speaking to classmates.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: You are presenting 'Thank You, Nurse' at the school clinic. Which opening line is best?
options: Good morning, nurse. Today I want to thank you for taking care of us.
Good morning, pupils. Let us talk about football.
Good morning, cook. The food is nice.
Good morning, driver. Thank you for driving.
hints: The audience is the nurse.
The purpose is to thank her.
questions.explanation: 'Good morning, nurse. Today I want to thank you for taking care of us' is the best opening because it addresses the nurse and states the purpose (thanking her). The others address different people or topics.
questions.misconception: Introduction and purpose are the same thing.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: Ama is presenting 'Our School Rules' to the whole school at assembly. She says, 'Good morning, my dear family. Today I will talk about my pet.' Which of these is the MAIN problem with her presentation?
options: She is speaking to the wrong audience and about the wrong topic.
She is not wearing a uniform.
She forgot to bring a microphone.
hints: Who should she be speaking to?
What should her topic be?
questions.explanation: The main problem is that she addresses her family instead of the whole school, and she says she will talk about her pet instead of school rules. The audience and purpose are both wrong.
questions.misconception: Introduction and purpose are the same thing.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: Kofi is presenting 'Why We Should Keep Our School Clean' to the whole school at assembly. He says, 'Good morning, teachers and pupils. Today I want to talk about how to play football.' What is wrong with his presentation?
options: The topic does not match the title or the purpose.
He is using the wrong microphone.
He is standing in the wrong place.
hints: What is the title of his presentation?
What does he say he will talk about?
questions.explanation: The problem is that his topic (how to play football) does not match the title ('Why We Should Keep Our School Clean') or the purpose. The audience is correct, but the purpose and topic are not.
questions.misconception: Any topic fits any audience.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Identify audience and purpose of presentation

questions.stem: Ama is presenting. She starts: 'My friend is kind. She helps me. I like her very much.' What is her topic?
hints: What is Ama talking about?
She is talking about someone she likes.
questions.explanation: Ama is talking about her friend — she says her friend is kind, helps her and that she likes her. So the topic is 'My friend'.
questions.misconception: The topic is the same as the title.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Generate and select ideas on a given topic for presentation e.g. My father, My friend, etc

questions.stem: Kofi is presenting. He says: 'My father is tall. He is a teacher. He helps me with my homework.' What is his topic?
hints: Who is Kofi talking about?
It is a member of his family.
questions.explanation: Kofi is talking about his father — he says his father is tall, is a teacher, and helps him with homework. So the topic is 'My father'.
questions.misconception: The topic is the same as the title.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Generate and select ideas on a given topic for presentation e.g. My father, My friend, etc

questions.stem: Your topic is 'My friend'. Which idea belongs in this presentation?
options: My friend is kind and helpful.
hints: The topic is a friend.
Which idea is about a friend?
questions.explanation: 'My friend is kind and helpful' belongs in a presentation about 'My friend'. The other ideas are about food, the school or the weather, so they do not belong.
questions.misconception: Any idea is relevant to any topic.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Generate and select ideas on a given topic for presentation e.g. My father, My friend, etc

questions.stem: Your topic is 'My pet'. Which idea does NOT belong?
hints: The topic is about a pet.
Which idea is not about a pet?
questions.explanation: 'I like going to school' is not about a pet, so it does not belong in a presentation titled 'My pet'. The other three ideas all describe a pet.

questions.objective: Generate and select ideas on a given topic for presentation e.g. My father, My friend, etc

answer: my school is near my house
my school has a big playing field
i have friends at my school
hints: What is your school like?
What do you like about it?
questions.explanation: Any idea that describes your school is correct. For example: 'My school is big', 'I like my school', or 'My school has a library'.

questions.stem: Your topic is 'My father'. Which idea is most relevant?
options: My father is a farmer and he grows maize.
hints: The topic is your father.
Which idea tells something about your father?
questions.explanation: 'My father is a farmer and he grows maize' is the most relevant idea because it tells something about your father. The other ideas are about food, the market or your school.
questions.misconception: 'My friend' and 'My father' can use the same exact ideas.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Generate and select ideas on a given topic for presentation e.g. My father, My friend, etc

questions.stem: Your topic is 'My school'. Which idea does NOT belong?
options: My school has a big library.
My school has a playing field.
hints: The topic is about school.
Which idea is not about school?
questions.explanation: 'My pet is a dog' is about a pet, not a school, so it does not belong in a presentation titled 'My school'. The other three ideas all describe things at school.
questions.misconception: Any idea is relevant to any topic.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Generate and select ideas on a given topic for presentation e.g. My father, My friend, etc

questions.stem: You are presenting 'My friend'. Which order makes the most sense?
options: What my friend likes → Who my friend is → Why I like my friend
Who my friend is → What my friend likes → Why I like my friend
Why I like my friend → What my friend likes → Who my friend is
What my friend likes → Why I like my friend → Who my friend is
hints: You usually say who first.
Then you add details, then why you like them.
questions.explanation: The most sensible order is: who my friend is (name), what my friend likes (details), and why I like my friend (reason). This gives the audience a clear picture of the friend.
questions.misconception: Presentation = listing ideas randomly.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Generate and select ideas on a given topic for presentation e.g. My father, My friend, etc

questions.stem: You are presenting 'My pet'. Which order is most sensible?
options: Why I like my pet → What my pet looks like → What my pet is
What my pet is → What my pet looks like → Why I like my pet
What my pet looks like → Why I like my pet → What my pet is
Why I like my pet → What my pet is → What my pet looks like
hints: What kind of pet is it? Then describe it. Then say why you like it.
questions.explanation: The sensible order is: what my pet is (dog, cat, goat), what my pet looks like (colour, size), and why I like my pet (reasons). This gives the audience a clear, logical picture.
questions.misconception: Presentation = listing ideas randomly.
questions.subject: English Language

questions.objective: Generate and select ideas on a given topic for presentation e.g. My father, My friend, etc

Which pair is entirely about your friend?
questions.explanation: Both 'My friend is kind' and 'My friend likes reading' are about the friend, so they are the most relevant pair. The other pairs contain ideas about other topics.
questions.misconception: Any idea is relevant to any topic.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Generate and select ideas on a given topic for presentation e.g. My father, My friend, etc

questions.stem: Which of these shows a pupil speaking with confidence?
options: Standing tall and looking at the audience
Looking at the floor and whispering
Turning your back to the audience
Covering your mouth with your hand
hints: Confident speakers stand up straight and look at their listeners.
They do not hide their face or their voice.
questions.explanation: Standing tall and looking at the audience shows confidence. Looking at the floor, turning your back or covering your mouth are signs of nervousness.
questions.misconception: Confidence means shouting.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Speak with confidence before different audiences, e.g. small group, class, etc

questions.stem: You are presenting to your whole class. How should you speak?
options: Very softly so only your friend hears
Loudly and clearly so everyone can hear
hints: The audience is the whole class.
Everyone needs to hear you.
questions.explanation: When presenting to the whole class, you need to speak loudly and clearly so everyone can hear. Whispering or speaking softly would make it hard for the class to hear you.
questions.misconception: Only some children can speak in front of the class.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Speak with confidence before different audiences, e.g. small group, class, etc

questions.stem: You feel nervous before your presentation. What is a good thing to do?
options: Take a deep breath and speak slowly
hints: Taking a breath helps you calm down.
Speaking slowly helps your voice stay steady.
questions.explanation: Taking a deep breath and speaking slowly help you calm down and speak clearly. Running away, crying or refusing to speak do not help you present.
questions.misconception: Nervousness means you cannot present.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Speak with confidence before different audiences, e.g. small group, class, etc

questions.stem: After Ama's presentation about 'My school', her teacher asks: 'What is your favourite place in the school?' What should Ama do?
hints: The teacher asked a question about the presentation.
Answer it politely.
questions.explanation: When someone asks a question after your presentation, you should answer it politely. Ignoring, walking away or crying are not appropriate responses.
questions.misconception: Answering questions after a presentation is not part of presenting.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Speak with confidence before different audiences, e.g. small group, class, etc

questions.stem: Write one thing a confident speaker does with their eyes.
hints: Confident speakers look at the people they are speaking to.
They do not look at the floor.
questions.explanation: A confident speaker looks at the audience or makes eye contact. This shows they are ready to share their ideas.
questions.misconception: Looking at the floor is fine.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Speak with confidence before different audiences, e.g. small group, class, etc

questions.stem: You are presenting to a small group of three friends. How should you speak?
options: Very loudly, like you are at assembly
Softly but clearly so the small group can hear
In a whisper so no one hears
hints: The audience is small.
You do not need to shout, but you need to be heard.
questions.explanation: For a small group, you can speak softly but clearly so everyone in the group can hear you. You do not need to shout like you would at assembly.
questions.misconception: Confidence means shouting.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Speak with confidence before different audiences, e.g. small group, class, etc

questions.stem: You feel nervous. Where is a good place to look to help you feel calm?
options: At a friendly face in the audience
hints: Looking at a friendly face can help you relax.
It is someone who supports you.
questions.explanation: Looking at a friendly face in the audience can help you feel calm and confident. Looking at the floor, ceiling or window does not help you connect with your audience.
questions.misconception: Nervousness means you cannot present.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Speak with confidence before different audiences, e.g. small group, class, etc

questions.stem: Present 'My friend' to a small group of three classmates. Speak clearly and look at your audience.

Speaks with confidence (stands tall, steady voice)

questions.stem: Which letter comes right after D?
hints: Say the alphabet: A, B, C, D...

questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Read level-appropriate sight words and use many of them in meaningful sentences

questions.stem: Which word means the same as 'one person'?
hints: It is a word you use when you talk about yourself.
It is a single capital letter.
questions.explanation: 'I' is the sight word for one person — yourself. 'You' is for the person you are speaking to, 'they' is for more than one person and 'we' is for a group including yourself.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'he' and 'she'.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Read level-appropriate sight words and use many of them in meaningful sentences

questions.stem: Choose the sight word that completes the sentence: '___ boy is my friend.' (He is a particular boy.)
hints: The sentence names a particular boy.
Which word points to a specific person?
questions.explanation: 'The boy is my friend' uses 'the' because it names a particular boy. 'A' is for any boy, 'an' is only used before a vowel sound, and 'some' is for more than one.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'the' and 'a'.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Read level-appropriate sight words and use many of them in meaningful sentences

questions.stem: Which sight word means the opposite of 'he'?
hints: 'He' is used for a boy.
What word is used for a girl?
questions.explanation: 'She' is the sight word used for a girl or woman, so it is the opposite of 'he'. 'It' is for an object, and 'we' and 'they' are for more than one person.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'he' and 'she'.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Read level-appropriate sight words and use many of them in meaningful sentences

questions.stem: Choose the sight word that completes the sentence: 'The boys ___ playing.'
hints: 'Boys' means more than one boy.
Which word goes with more than one?
questions.explanation: 'Are' goes with 'the boys' because 'boys' is plural (more than one). 'Is' goes with one person (the boy is). 'Am' goes with 'I' and 'be' does not fit here.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'is' and 'are'.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Read level-appropriate sight words and use many of them in meaningful sentences

questions.stem: Choose the sight word that completes the sentence: 'My mother is a nurse. ___ is kind.'
hints: The sentence is about your mother.
Which word do we use for a woman?
questions.explanation: 'She' is used for a woman. Since the sentence is about the mother, 'She is kind' is correct. 'He' is for a man, 'it' is for an object and 'they' is for more than one.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'he' and 'she'.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Read level-appropriate sight words and use many of them in meaningful sentences

questions.stem: Choose the sight word that completes the sentence: '___ child is my sister.' (Use the word that points to a particular child.)

questions.misconception: Confusing 'the' and 'a'.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Read level-appropriate sight words and use many of them in meaningful sentences

questions.misconception: Confusing 'is' and 'are'.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Read level-appropriate sight words and use many of them in meaningful sentences

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct sight word: 'This is ___ table in my house.' (The table is a particular one.)

questions.stem: Read: 'Kwame washed his hands. He sat at the table. He ate his lunch.' How did the text end?
hints: What is the last action in the text?
It is something to do with food.
questions.explanation: The last action is Kwame eating his lunch. Washing his hands and sitting at the table happen before.
questions.misconception: The beginning is the end.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama woke up. She washed her face. She went to school.' Which order is correct?
options: Washed her face → Woke up → Went to school
Went to school → Woke up → Washed her face
Ama woke up → Washed her face → Went to school
Ama woke up → Went to school → Washed her face
hints: What is the first thing Ama did?
Washing comes before going to school.
questions.explanation: The text order is: she woke up, then washed her face, then went to school. Only option 3 follows this order.
questions.misconception: Order does not matter in a retell.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi went to the market. He bought a mango. He ate the mango. He went home.' Which order is correct?
options: Went to market → Ate the mango → Bought the mango → Went home
Went to market → Bought the mango → Ate the mango → Went home
Went home → Went to market → Bought the mango → Ate the mango
Bought the mango → Went to market → Ate the mango → Went home
hints: What did Kofi do first?
He must buy the mango before he eats it.
questions.explanation: Kofi goes to the market first, then buys a mango, then eats it, then goes home. Only option 2 follows this order.
questions.misconception: Order does not matter in a retell.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama went to the river to fetch water. The pot was heavy. She rested under a tree. A kind woman helped her carry the pot. Ama thanked her.' What is the most important event in the text?
options: Ama fetched water from the river
The kind woman helped Ama carry the pot
hints: What solved Ama's problem?
The pot was too heavy for her.
questions.explanation: Ama's problem was the heavy pot. The key event is when the kind woman helps her carry it. Resting and thanking are smaller parts of the text.
questions.misconception: A small detail is the key event.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi lost his pencil. He looked under the table. He looked in his bag. Ama said, "Here is your pencil. It fell near the door." Kofi was happy.' What is the key event?
hints: What solved Kofi's problem?
He could not find his pencil.
questions.explanation: Kofi's problem was losing his pencil. The key event is when Ama finds it and tells him where it was. Looking under the table and in his bag did not solve the problem.
questions.misconception: A small detail is the key event.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama found a small bird. The bird had a hurt wing. Ama put the bird in a box. She gave it food and water. The bird got well and flew away.' Which is the key event?
options: The bird had a hurt wing
The bird got well and flew away
Ama put the bird in a box
hints: Which event changes the story the most?
It is the end of the problem.
questions.explanation: The key event is when the bird gets well and flies away. This shows that all of Ama's care worked. The other events are steps along the way.
questions.misconception: The first event is the key event.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi found a coin on the road. He picked it up. He put it in his pocket. He bought sweets with it. He shared the sweets with his sister.' How did the text end?
options: Kofi shared sweets with his sister
Kofi put the coin in his pocket
hints: What is the last thing that happened?
It involves his sister.
questions.explanation: The last action is Kofi sharing the sweets with his sister. Finding the coin, picking it up and putting it in the pocket happen before.
questions.misconception: The start is the ending.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama woke up early. She washed her face. She ate her food. She went to school.' Which event was NOT in the text?
hints: Which event is not in the text?
Think about where Ama went after eating.
questions.explanation: The text says Ama woke up, washed her face, ate her food and went to school. Playing football is not in the text.
questions.misconception: Any event from another story can fit.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi went to the market. He bought a mango. He ate the mango. He went home.' Which event was NOT in the text?
hints: Did Kofi buy or sell the mango?
Read the text carefully.
questions.explanation: The text says Kofi bought a mango, not sold one. Selling is not in the text.
questions.misconception: Any event from another story can fit.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama woke up early. She washed her face. She ate her food. She went to school.' Retell the text in your own words.

criteria.description: Tells what Ama did in the correct order
Uses own words (not just repeating exactly)

hints: Start with what Ama did first.
Use your own words.
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for a retell in the correct order, using own words and clear speech.
questions.misconception: Retelling means repeating every word exactly.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi went to the market. He bought a mango. He ate the mango. He went home.' Retell the text in your own words, in the correct order.

criteria.description: Retells the events in the correct order
Includes all the key events (market, mango, ate, home)

hints: Start with where Kofi went.
Then say what he did.
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for correct order, key events and own words.
questions.misconception: Retelling means repeating every word exactly.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama went to the river to fetch water. The pot was heavy. She rested under a tree. A kind woman helped her carry the pot. Ama thanked her.' Retell the text in your own words. Include the beginning, middle and end.

criteria.description: Tells the beginning (Ama went to the river)
Tells the middle (the pot was heavy, she rested)
Tells the end (a woman helped and Ama thanked her)
Uses own words and speaks clearly

hints: What did Ama do first?
What went wrong?
How did it end?
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for beginning, middle and end in order, using own words.
questions.misconception: Order does not matter in a retell.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'A greedy dog found a piece of meat. He was crossing a river. He saw another dog in the water with a bigger piece of meat. He opened his mouth to grab it. His own meat fell into the water. The greedy dog lost his meat.' Retell the text in your own words. At the end, say what lesson the story teaches.

criteria.description: Retells the text in the correct order
Includes the key event (the dog lost his meat)
States a clear lesson (do not be greedy)

hints: Think about what the dog saw in the water.
What happened when he opened his mouth?
questions.explanation: This is an extended oral task. The teacher listens for correct order, the key event, a moral lesson and clear speech.
questions.misconception: A retell can skip the lesson.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama found a small bird with a hurt wing. She put it in a box. She gave it food and water. The bird got well and flew away.' Which event was NOT in the text?
options: Ama put the bird in a box
The bird got well and flew away
Ama sold the bird at the market
hints: What did Ama do with the bird?
Did she sell it?
questions.explanation: The text says Ama found the bird, put it in a box, gave it food and water, and the bird flew away. There is no mention of selling the bird.
questions.misconception: Any event from another story can fit.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'The rain started. Ama ran home. She was wet. She changed her clothes. Her mother made her warm tea.' Which event was NOT in the text?
hints: What did Ama do when it rained?
Did she go anywhere else?
questions.explanation: The text says the rain started, Ama ran home, she was wet, changed her clothes and her mother made tea. Going to the market is not in the text.
questions.misconception: Any event from another story can fit.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi was walking to school. He saw a small bag on the ground. He picked it up. There was money inside. He took it to the teacher.' What is the most important event in the text? Say it aloud.

criteria.description: Identifies the key event (Kofi found the bag and took it to the teacher)
Explains why it is important (it shows honesty)

hints: What did Kofi do that was important?
Why is his action important?
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for identification of the key event and a simple explanation.
questions.misconception: A small detail is the key event.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: Read: 'Maame Adwoa sold oranges at the market. Every day, Yaw bought two oranges. One day Yaw did not come. Maame Adwoa learned Yaw was sick. She took oranges to Yaw's house. Yaw's mother thanked her.' Retell how the text ended in your own words.

criteria.description: Says Maame Adwoa took oranges to Yaw's house
Uses own words and speaks clearly

hints: What did Maame Adwoa do for Yaw?
What did Yaw's mother do?
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for the ending of the text retold in own words.
questions.misconception: A retell can skip the end.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

questions.stem: What is a narrative text for?
options: To give a list of facts
hints: Narrative comes from the word for 'story'.
What do you do when someone tells you a story?
questions.explanation: A narrative text is for telling a story. Giving facts, showing a recipe or giving instructions are other purposes for other types of text.
questions.misconception: Narratives have no purpose.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama went to the market with her mother. They bought rice and beans.' Who is the character in this story?
hints: Who is the person in the story?
A character is a person or animal in the story.
questions.explanation: Ama is the character because she is the person in the story. The market is the setting, and the rice and beans are objects.
questions.misconception: Narratives only have characters.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Kofi is reading a story about a lion and an ant. Why did the writer write this story?
options: To tell a story and entertain
To explain how to play a game
hints: The story is about a lion and an ant — a made-up story.
What is the purpose of a made-up story?
questions.explanation: A story about a lion and an ant is a narrative. The writer wrote it to tell a story and entertain readers, not to give facts or instructions.
questions.misconception: The purpose of a narrative is to give facts.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi found a small bird under a tree.' What is the SETTING of this story?
hints: The setting is WHERE the story happens.
Where did Kofi find the bird?
questions.explanation: The setting is where the story happens: under a tree. Kofi and the bird are characters, and finding is an event.
questions.misconception: Narratives only have characters.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Write one thing a narrative text is for.
hints: It has characters and events.
It is a made-up story.
questions.explanation: A narrative text is for telling a story or entertaining the reader.
questions.misconception: The purpose of a narrative is to give facts.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama found a small bird. The bird had a hurt wing. Ama put it in a box. The bird got well.' What is the PROBLEM in this story?
options: The bird has a hurt wing
hints: What went wrong in the story?
What is the bird's condition?
questions.explanation: The problem in the story is that the bird has a hurt wing. The story is about Ama helping the bird get better.
questions.misconception: Narratives only have characters.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama found a small bird with a hurt wing. She put it in a box and gave it food. The bird got well and flew away.' What is the SOLUTION in this story?
options: Ama put the bird in a box and gave it food
Ama gave the bird to someone else
Ama left the bird on the road
hints: How was the problem solved?
What did Ama do to help the bird?
questions.explanation: The solution is Ama putting the bird in a box and giving it food, which helped the bird get well and fly away.
questions.misconception: Narratives only have characters.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi went to the market. He bought a mango. He ate it. He went home.' Which feature of a narrative does this text have?
hints: Who is in the story? What happens?
A narrative has characters and events.
questions.explanation: This text has a character (Kofi) and events (going to the market, buying, eating, going home). Lists, instructions and recipes are not narratives.
questions.misconception: Narratives only have characters.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Which of these is a narrative text?
options: A story about Ananse and the wisdom pot
hints: A narrative tells a story.
Which one has characters and events?
questions.explanation: A story about Ananse is a narrative because it has characters and events. A recipe, a list of rules and instructions are not narratives.
questions.misconception: Every text is a narrative.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Which of these is a narrative text?
options: A story about a kind girl named Ama
A list of items to buy at the market
A letter to a friend about school
A set of instructions for drawing a house
hints: A narrative tells a story.
Which one has a character and events?
questions.explanation: A story about a kind girl named Ama is a narrative. It has a character and events that tell a story.
questions.misconception: Every text is a narrative.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi went to the market. He bought a mango.' Which feature of a narrative is MISSING from this text?
hints: Does the text tell about something going wrong?
Is there a problem to be solved?
questions.explanation: The text has characters (Kofi), events (going to the market, buying) and setting (the market). But there is no problem and no solution. Problem and solution are features of many narratives.
questions.misconception: Narratives only have characters.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama is my friend. She is kind. She helps me.' Is this a narrative?
options: Yes, it is a story about Ama
No, it describes a person, it does not tell a story with events
hints: Does it tell a story with a problem and events?
It only describes Ama.
questions.explanation: This is not a narrative. It describes Ama, but it does not tell a story with events, a problem and a solution. A narrative needs a story with events.
questions.misconception: Every text is a narrative.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama went to the river. The pot was heavy. She rested under a tree. A kind woman helped her.' Which feature matches the sentence 'Ama went to the river'?
hints: The sentence tells WHERE the story happens.
Where did Ama go?
questions.explanation: The sentence 'Ama went to the river' tells us the setting (where the story happens).
questions.misconception: Narratives only have characters.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama went to the river. The pot was heavy. She rested under a tree. A kind woman helped her carry the pot.' Which feature matches 'the pot was heavy'?
hints: This sentence shows what went wrong.
Is it a problem for Ama?
questions.explanation: The sentence 'the pot was heavy' describes the problem in the story. The solution is when the kind woman helps carry the pot.
questions.misconception: Narratives only have characters.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama went to the river. The pot was heavy. She rested under a tree. A kind woman helped her carry the pot.' Which feature matches 'a kind woman helped her carry the pot'?
hints: This sentence solves the problem.
What happens after the problem?
questions.explanation: 'A kind woman helped her carry the pot' is the solution. It fixes Ama's problem with the heavy pot.
questions.misconception: Narratives only have characters.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Say what a narrative text is for and name two features of a narrative.

criteria.description: Says a narrative tells a story or entertains
Names at least two features (characters, setting, events, problem, solution)

hints: What is a narrative?
Think about characters, setting, events.
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for the purpose and at least two features of a narrative.
questions.misconception: Narratives have no purpose.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama found a small bird with a hurt wing. She put it in a box and fed it. The bird got well and flew away.' Say what a narrative is for and name two features you can find in this story.

criteria.description: Says a narrative tells a story or entertains
Names at least two features from the story (characters, setting, problem, solution, events)
Explains why the story is a narrative

hints: Who is in the story?
What was the problem?
How was it solved?
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for the purpose, the features found in the story and a clear explanation.
questions.misconception: Narratives only have characters.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi lost his pencil. He looked under the table and in his bag. Ama found it and gave it to him. Kofi was happy.' Say what a narrative is for and name two features of this narrative.

criteria.description: Says a narrative tells a story or entertains
Names at least two features (characters, problem, solution, events)

hints: Who is in the story?
What was the problem?
How was it solved?
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for the purpose and two features of the narrative.
questions.misconception: Narratives have no purpose.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Read: 'A greedy dog found a piece of meat. He saw another dog in the water with a bigger piece. He opened his mouth to grab it. His own meat fell into the water.' Say what a narrative is for. Name three features of this narrative and explain why this story is a narrative.

criteria.description: Says a narrative tells a story or entertains
Names three features (characters, setting, events, problem, solution)
Explains why the story is a narrative (it has characters and events, it tells a story with a lesson)

hints: Who is the character?
Where does the story take place?
What is the problem and the lesson?
questions.explanation: This is an extended oral task. The teacher listens for the purpose, three features and a clear explanation.
questions.misconception: Every text is a narrative.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of narrative texts

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama is a tall girl with short hair. She is kind and helpful.' Which sentence describes Ama?
options: Ama is a tall girl with short hair.
hints: Look for the sentence that tells what Ama looks like.
It mentions her height and hair.
questions.explanation: 'Ama is a tall girl with short hair' describes what Ama looks like. The other options are wrong or do not describe her.
questions.misconception: Description = name only.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe characters and their actions in a story

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi found a small bird with a hurt wing. He put it in a box and gave it food.' What did Kofi do?
options: He found a bird and cared for it
hints: What did Kofi do with the bird?
He put it in a box and fed it.
questions.explanation: Kofi found the bird and cared for it by putting it in a box and feeding it.
questions.misconception: Characters only do one thing.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe characters and their actions in a story

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama was walking home. She saw a small bird. The bird had a hurt wing. Ama helped the bird.' Who is the main character?
hints: Who is the story mostly about?
Who is doing the helping?
questions.explanation: Ama is the main character because the story is mostly about her and what she did to help the bird.
questions.misconception: The main character is always the first one mentioned.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe characters and their actions in a story

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi lost his pencil. He looked everywhere but could not find it. He was very sad.' How did Kofi feel?
hints: The text says he was very ___.
He lost something.
questions.explanation: The text says Kofi was very sad because he lost his pencil.
questions.misconception: Feelings are not part of a character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe characters and their actions in a story

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama went to the market. She bought a mango. She ate it.' What did Ama buy?
hints: Look for what Ama bought.
It is a fruit.
questions.explanation: The text says Ama bought a mango.
questions.misconception: Characters only do one thing.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe characters and their actions in a story

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi is a tall boy. He has short black hair. He is very kind.' Which sentence BEST describes Kofi?
hints: What does the text say about Kofi?
He is tall and kind.
questions.explanation: The text says Kofi is tall and kind. The other options do not match the text.
questions.misconception: Description = name only.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe characters and their actions in a story

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama found a small bird with a hurt wing. She put it in a box and gave it food. The bird got well and flew away.' What did Ama do to help the bird?
options: She put it in a box and gave it food
She left it on the road
She gave it to someone else
hints: What did Ama do after finding the bird?
She put it in a box and fed it.
questions.explanation: Ama put the bird in a box and gave it food. This helped the bird get well.
questions.misconception: Characters only do one thing.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe characters and their actions in a story

questions.stem: Read: 'The lion was big and proud. He laughed at the small ant. One day the lion was caught in a net. The ant came with many ants and cut the net. The lion was free.' Who is the main character?
hints: Who is the story mostly about?
The story starts and ends with this character.
questions.explanation: The lion is the main character. The story is about the lion being proud, getting caught in a net and being freed by the ant.
questions.misconception: The main character is always the first one mentioned.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe characters and their actions in a story

questions.stem: Read: 'The lion was big and proud. He laughed at the small ant. One day the lion was caught in a net. The ant came with many ants and cut the net. The lion was free.' What did the lion do?
options: He laughed at the ant and got caught in a net
He helped the ant find food
He ran away from the forest
hints: What did the lion do at the beginning?
What happened to the lion later?
questions.explanation: The lion laughed at the ant and later got caught in a net. The ant helped free him.
questions.misconception: Characters only do one thing.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe characters and their actions in a story

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama found a small bird with a hurt wing. She put it in a box and gave it food. The bird got well and flew away. Ama was very happy.' How did Ama feel at the end?
hints: The text says Ama was very ___.
The bird got well.
questions.explanation: Ama was very happy at the end because the bird got well and flew away.
questions.misconception: Feelings are not part of a character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe characters and their actions in a story

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi lost his pencil. He looked under the table and in his bag. He could not find it. He was sad.' How did Kofi feel?
hints: The text says he was ___ because he lost his pencil.
It starts with 's'.
questions.explanation: The text says Kofi was sad because he lost his pencil.
questions.misconception: Feelings are not part of a character.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe characters and their actions in a story

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama went to the market. She bought a mango. She ate it on the way home.' Which action did Ama NOT do?
hints: What did Ama buy?
Did she buy a ball?
questions.explanation: The text says Ama bought a mango, not a ball. So 'She bought a ball' is the action she did not do.
questions.misconception: Actions from other stories fit.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe characters and their actions in a story

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi found a small bird with a hurt wing. He put it in a box and gave it food. The bird got well and flew away.' Which action did Kofi NOT do?
options: He put it in a box
hints: What did Kofi do with the bird?
Did he sell it?
questions.explanation: The text says Kofi found the bird, put it in a box and gave it food. He did not sell it.
questions.misconception: Actions from other stories fit.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe characters and their actions in a story

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama is a tall girl with short hair. She is very kind. She helps her mother at home.' Describe Ama in one or two sentences.

criteria.description: Says at least one thing about Ama's appearance
Says at least one thing about her character

hints: What does Ama look like?
What kind of person is she?
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for a description that includes appearance and character.
questions.misconception: Description = name only.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe characters and their actions in a story

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi found a small bird with a hurt wing. He put it in a box and gave it food. The bird got well and flew away. Kofi was happy.' Describe Kofi and what he did in the story.

criteria.description: Says what Kofi did (found the bird, put it in a box, fed it)
Says how Kofi felt at the end (happy)

hints: Who is the character?
What did he do?
How did he feel?
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for a description of Kofi, his actions and his feelings.
questions.misconception: Description = name only.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Describe characters and their actions in a story

questions.stem: Read: 'The lion was big and proud. He laughed at the small ant. One day the lion was caught in a net. The ant came with many ants and cut the net. The lion was free.' Describe the lion and what he did in the story.

criteria.description: Says what the lion did (laughed at the ant, got caught in a net)
Says how the lion felt at the end (free/thankful)

hints: What does the lion look like?
What did the lion do?
How did he feel at the end?
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for a description of the lion, his actions and his feelings.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama found a small bird with a hurt wing. She put it in a box and fed it. The bird got well and flew away.' Which labels are in the correct order?

What happened last?

What happened last?

questions.subject: English Language

questions.stem: Which is the best pace for reading a short sentence?
options: Very fast, rushing through the words
Very slow, one word at a time
A steady pace, not too fast and not too slow
Reading without looking at the words
hints: Good reading is not too fast and not too slow.
You want people to understand you.
questions.explanation: The best pace is steady — not too fast and not too slow. Rushing makes it hard to understand, and reading word-by-word is too slow.
questions.misconception: Fast = good reading.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Read short and simple sentences at good pace

questions.stem: Which reader is reading at a good pace?

Kofi reads slowly, one word at a time.
Adjoa reads each word clearly at a steady speed.
Yaw reads without looking at the book.
hints: Good pace means clear and steady.
Which reader can you understand best?
questions.explanation: Adjoa reads each word clearly at a steady speed, which is a good pace. Ama reads too fast, Kofi reads too slowly and Yaw is not reading at all.
questions.misconception: Fast = good reading.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Read short and simple sentences at good pace

questions.stem: Should you read a sentence very fast or at a steady pace? Write your answer.
answer: not too fast and not too slow
hints: Good reading is not too fast and not too slow.

questions.explanation: You should read at a steady pace — not too fast and not too slow — so that listeners can understand you.
questions.misconception: Fast = good reading.
questions.subject: English Language
questions.objective: Read short and simple sentences at good pace

questions.stem: Which is the best way to read this sentence? 'The boy / is playing / with the ball.'

The boy is playing with the ball (very fast)
The boy... is... playing... with... the... ball
hints: Good readers read groups of words together.
It sounds natural, not choppy.
questions.explanation: Reading in phrases like 'The boy / is playing / with the ball' sounds natural and helps listeners understand. Reading word-by-word or very fast does not.
questions.misconception: Reading every word separately is correct.

questions.stem: How should your voice change when you read a sentence with a question mark?

It is the opposite of a full stop.
questions.explanation: When you read a question, your voice goes up at the end. This shows that you are asking something, not making a statement.
questions.misconception: A question mark does not change the voice.

questions.stem: When you read a sentence with a full stop at the end, what should you do with your voice?

questions.explanation: When you read a sentence with a full stop, your voice goes down and you pause briefly before the next sentence. This helps listeners understand where one sentence ends and the next begins.

questions.stem: Which pattern is made of straight lines that go up and down?

questions.stem: What should you do after reading a book from the library?
hints: Library books belong to everyone.
Return them so others can read.
questions.explanation: You should return the book to the shelf so others can read it too.
questions.misconception: Books must be finished in one sitting.

questions.stem: Write one good reading habit.
hints: What should you do with books?
How often should you read?
questions.explanation: Any good reading habit is correct, for example reading every day or returning books to the shelf.
questions.misconception: Reading is only for school.

questions.stem: Choose a picture book from the reading corner. Read it quietly for two minutes.

criteria.description: Reads or looks at the book quietly
Stays on task for the time given

hints: Choose a book you like.
Look at the pictures and read the words.
questions.explanation: This is a practical reading task. The teacher watches the pupil choose and read a book.
questions.misconception: Picture books are not real reading.

questions.stem: Choose a book with a partner. Take turns reading a page each.

criteria.description: Chooses a book with a partner

hints: Take turns reading.
Listen to your partner.
questions.explanation: This is a practical reading task. The teacher watches the pair read together.
questions.misconception: Reading silently is not reading.

questions.stem: Choose a book from the reading corner and read it on your own for three minutes. Then tell your teacher one thing from the book.

criteria.description: Tells one thing from the book

hints: Read quietly.
Remember one thing to tell your teacher.
questions.explanation: This is a practical reading task. The teacher watches the pupil read and then listens to one thing from the book.

questions.stem: Choose a book you have not read before. Read it on your own for five minutes. Then tell your teacher what it was about.

criteria.description: Tells what the book was about

hints: Choose a book you have not read.
Read quietly and remember what happens.
questions.explanation: This is a practical reading task. The teacher watches the pupil read and listens to a summary.
questions.misconception: Books must be finished in one sitting.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher the name of a book you read and one thing you liked about it.
hints: Think about a book you enjoyed.
Say what you liked.
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for the book name and a reason for liking it.
questions.misconception: Only the teacher can choose books.

questions.stem: Talk about a book you read. Say what it was about and what you liked best.

criteria.description: Says what the book was about

hints: What happened in the book?
What was your favourite part?
questions.explanation: This is an oral task. The teacher listens for a description and a preference.

questions.stem: Tell the class about a book you read this week. Say the title, what it was about, and why you would or would not tell a friend to read it.

criteria.description: Says what the book was about
Gives a reason for recommending or not recommending it

hints: Think about a book you read this week.
Would you tell a friend to read it?
questions.explanation: This is an extended oral task. The teacher listens for a summary and a recommendation.
